title: Evenstar takes flight
body_text: 29 OCT 2025 -- Our team just hit a major milestone: Maiden flight of Evensta r , our full-scale stratospheric aircraft prototype (what we call StratoSats). StratoSats are a new class of solar-powered, autonomous aircraft built to operate in the stratosphere. This first flight validated our rapid design, simulation, and build process, proving we can go from concept to full-scale flight in just a few months. At Radical, our mission is to build enduring infrastructure in the sky. Evenstar represents a key step toward that vision. With a 120-foot wingspan, a 15-kilogram payload capacity, and a total mass of 110 kilograms, it demonstrates the lightweight, energy-efficient design required for continuous stratospheric flight. Over the coming months, we’ll continue expanding flight operations as we prepare for high-altitude testing in 2026. Each flight brings us closer to demonstrating persistent, solar-powered connectivity and imaging from near space. It’s truly remarkable what our lean team has achieved in just a few months. The skies are opening, and the potential to connect and observe our planet sustainably has never been greater. – James & Cyriel

title: Three Trends That Will Shape the Next Phase of Retail Media in ANZ
summary: What NORA’s 2026 State of Play report reveals about the opportunities and barriers shaping ANZ retail media growth.
body_text: Table of contents Measurement must move beyond ROAS Agency activation is the next growth lever Reducing friction will unlock larger budgets The bottom line Retail media in Australia and New Zealand is growing quickly, but its next phase will depend on how effectively the market can move past uneven maturity, operational friction and unanswered measurement questions. As a partner of NORA’s 2026 State of Play report, Criteo had the opportunity to examine these challenges through input from more than 60 brands, retailers and practitioners across the market. The report offers a clear snapshot of where the market stands today and what retailers need to address as they build more mature, measurable and scalable retail media businesses. In this blog post, we look at three findings from the report and what they mean for retail media marketers looking to unlock the next stage of growth in ANZ. Measurement must move beyond ROAS Measurement remains one of the ANZ market’s defining challenges. Across survey groups and interview cohorts, it emerged as the most consistent constraint on future growth, with the industry increasingly aligned that attribution and ROAS alone are no longer enough. Retail media is now expected to answer a more commercially important question: whether the media drove genuinely incremental growth. That expectation is rising because retail media increasingly serves multiple audiences at once. Trade teams may want sell-through and distribution proof, while marketing and agency teams want incrementality, brand impact and full-funnel performance. Yet many retailers are still trying to serve these needs through a single measurement framework. From a Criteo perspective, ROAS remains a useful baseline, but it can’t deliver the proof of incrementality that brands, agencies, and CFOs now require. That’s why measurement needs to evolve beyond isolated platform reporting toward more transparent, credible and comparable frameworks. The networks that build confidence will be the ones that can connect exposure to outcomes with greater rigour, bring together online and in-store signals where possible, and provide metrics that stand up against the same scrutiny applied to other media channels. Incrementality should not be treated as a future enhancement. It needs to sit at the core of retail media measurement if the category is going to attract larger and more durable budgets. Agency activation is the next growth lever NORA’s findings make clear that, in ANZ, retail media still often sits structurally outside the agency ecosystem. It is frequently briefed too late, bought differently and measured separately from the rest of the media plan, leaving it adjacent to broader planning rather than fully integrated within it. Agencies are also often brought into the conversation after creative and budget decisions have already been made. That makes retail media harder to operationalise within standard workflows and means agency budgets remain underrepresented. From a Criteo standpoint, agency activation is one of the clearest levers for unlocking incremental budgets beyond reallocated trade spend. Retail media will scale faster when brands and agencies can brief, buy and measure it without having to work around bespoke processes or unfamiliar reporting standards. That means retail media networks increasingly need to operate more like media owners, with stronger analytics, transparent data, accredited media and better integration into broader planning and activation workflows. As retail media becomes easier to compare, easier to activate and easier to measure alongside other channels, it becomes a more natural destination for broader brand and media budgets, rather than simply absorbing spend that already existed inside retailer relationships. Reducing friction will unlock larger budgets The report also indicates that demand is not the limiting factor for market growth. Media buyer appetite already exceeds what many retailers are equipped to service, particularly across early and mid-stage operators where the real constraints are resourcing, workflow maturity, data integration and internal coordination. This is closely connected to another key finding: ANZ is not one market moving through a single maturity curve. Some retailers are still determining whether retail media should exist as a dedicated function, while others are already dealing with oversubscribed demand, advanced measurement needs and growing non-endemic revenue. At the same time, much of the market’s recent growth has come from formalising existing trade and brand investment, with truly incremental advertiser budgets typically appearing only once stronger measurement and commercial foundations are in place. From what we’re seeing, operational simplicity will become a major competitive advantage as brands spread investment across more retail media networks. The challenge is not simply building more technology. It is removing the friction that slows activation, optimisation, reporting and decision-making across fragmented ecosystems. Retailers need to meet media buyers where they already work, through self-service tools, APIs and other workflow integrations that make campaigns easier to run and easier to scale. The opportunity is not to give up control, but to reduce complexity while preserving pricing, inventory, shopper experience and direct commercial relationships. The retailers that simplify operations most effectively will be best positioned to unlock larger, more incremental budgets, rather than simply reshuffling spend already in market. The bottom line The NORA research makes one thing clear: the next phase of retail media growth in ANZ will not be driven by inventory expansion alone. It will be shaped by better measurement, stronger agency integration and lower operational friction. Retailers that can make retail media easier to prove, easier to buy and easier to scale will be in the strongest position to attract the next wave of investment. title: Pagos a empleadas domésticas antes de fin de año: guía práctica

body_text: Pagos a empleadas domésticas antes de fin de año: guía práctica Publicado el 1 de Diciembre de 2025 por Equipo de crecimiento La llegada de diciembre también marca el momento ideal para revisar los pagos a empleadas domésticas antes de fin de año . Cumplir con las prestaciones y obligaciones pendientes te permitirá cerrar el año con tranquilidad y garantizar que quienes te ayudan en casa disfruten unas fiestas justas y sin preocupaciones. En esta guía te contamos todo lo que debes saber sobre los pagos a empleadas domésticas antes de fin de año, incluyendo prima, cesantías, vacaciones y liquidación proporcional. 1. ¿Quiénes son considerados trabajadores domésticos? Define qué se entiende legalmente por “empleada doméstica” (externa, interna, por días, por horas) y aclara que todas tienen derechos laborales, sin importar la modalidad. Esto aplica incluso si trabajan por días o pocas horas. Diario ADN+2Colombia.com+2 2. Obligaciones laborales que deben estar al día Incluye tener un vínculo laboral (contrato verbal o escrito), reconocer salario mínimo o superior, respetar jornadas, y garantizar afiliación a seguridad social (salud, pensión, riesgos profesionales). Colombia.com+2Universidad de la Sabana+2 3. Pagos a empleadas domésticas antes de fin de año: lo que sí o sí debes liquidar Describe las prestaciones y pagos obligatorios: Ley 1788 de 2016 : otorga a las trabajadoras domésticas el derecho a prima de servicios. ICEF+2Comfama+2 Prima de servicios : corresponde a 30 días de salario por año, pagada en dos cuotas — la segunda antes del 20 de diciembre. ICEF+1 Cesantías : un mes de salario por cada año trabajado (o proporcional al tiempo trabajado). Accounter+2Accounter+2 Intereses sobre cesantías : se deben pagar al finalizar el año (o contrato), proporcionales si no completó año. Accounter+1 Vacaciones remuneradas : 15 días hábiles por año, o compensación proporcional si no se disfrutan. Universidad de la Sabana+2Comfama+2 Dotación (vestido y calzado de labor) , cuando aplique — obligatorio si la jornada o el salario lo requieren. La Opinión+2LitiApp Directorio de Abogados+2 Afiliación y cotización a seguridad social (salud, pensión, riesgos laborales). Colombia.com+2Diario Occidente+2 4. Cómo calcular los pagos a empleadas domésticas antes de fin de año . 1. ¿Cómo se calcula la prima de servicios? La prima equivale a un mes de salario por año , pero si la empleada no ha trabajado todo el periodo, se calcula así: (Salario mensual × días trabajados en el semestre) / 360 . Esto permite pagar solo la parte proporcional según el tiempo laborado. 2. ¿Cómo se calculan las cesantías? Las cesantías corresponden a un mes de salario por cada año trabajado , o proporcional si no ha cumplido el año completo. Fórmula básica: (Salario mensual × días trabajados en todo el año) / 360 . 3. ¿Cómo se calculan los intereses de cesantías? Son el 12% anual sobre el valor de las cesantías acumuladas. Si la empleada no trabajó todo el año, se calculan proporcionalmente a los días laborados. 4. ¿Cómo se calculan las vacaciones? La empleada doméstica tiene derecho a 15 días hábiles de vacaciones por año . Si trabajó menos, se calculan así: Salario devengado (sin auxilio de transporte) x días trabajados/720 Eso indica cuántos días de descanso o pago proporcional le corresponden. 5. ¿Cómo se calcula cuando la empleada trabaja por días? Si la empleada trabaja solo algunos días a la semana, todo se calcula proporcionalmente : Se aplica la misma fórmula de 360 días para prima, cesantías y vacaciones. Esto garantiza que reciba lo justo según el tiempo real de servicio. Se toma el total de días efectivamente trabajados. 6. ¿Cómo se calcula una liquidación si el contrato termina? La liquidación incluye todos los valores proporcionales pendientes: Prima Cesantías Intereses de cesantías Vacaciones Salario de los últimos días trabajados Si aplica, también se incluyen indemnizaciones por terminación sin justa causa. 💡 ¿Y si no sabes cómo calcular todo esto? title: Beyond recognition: what industry awards say about Banking
summary: In banking and capital markets, awards are about more than recognition – they provide a snapshot of market’s evolution, highlighting the transactions, solutions and institutions that are helping advance innovation and support economic growth.
body_text: Back to News Beyond recognition: what industry awards say about Banking Share Email LinkedIn Twitter In banking and capital markets, awards are about more than recognition – they provide a snapshot of market’s evolution, highlighting the transactions, solutions and institutions that are helping advance innovation and support economic growth. The industry's most respected awards are judged not only on financial performance, but also on the complexity of transactions, the creativity of financing structures, the quality of execution and the value delivered to clients. Deal of the Year awards often recognise transactions that open new markets, pioneer innovative financing approaches or establish new standards for the industry. For investment banks, this recognition is therefore less about celebrating individual achievements and more about demonstrating the ability to solve increasingly sophisticated client challenges. Whether supporting the energy transition, financing critical infrastructure, facilitating international trade or providing access to capital across public and private markets, the common denominator is the capacity to bring together expertise, execution and long-term relationships. This is particularly relevant at a time when clients expect more than financing. Companies, financial institutions and governments are looking for partners that can combine sector knowledge, global connectivity and innovative thinking to deliver solutions that create long-term value. The industry's leading awards increasingly reflect this evolution, recognising not only the scale of transactions but also their broader economic and strategic impact. During the first half of 2026, Santander Corporate & Investment Banking was recognised by a number of the industry's leading publications – including LatinFinance, IJGlobal, Global Capital, Global Banking & Markets, Global Finance, TMI, GTR, TMT Finance and The Asset – across areas such as debt capital markets, infrastructure, transaction banking, trade finance and payments. Together they illustrate the breadth of Santander CIB's platform and the collaborative work carried out across teams, products and geographies to support clients worldwide. title: FAANG, MBB, and Elite Banking: Do Prestigious Employers Predict PE CEO Success?
summary: The market knowledge your talent decisions depend on — centralized. Verata unifies company intelligence, executive data, and search management in one platform built for PE talent and executive search.
body_text: Across all three pedigree categories — FAANG, MBB, and elite banking — the results converge on the same conclusion: prestigious prior employers do not predict PE-backed CEO success. FAANG experience is slightly negative, MBB is promising but insignificant, and elite banking is a complete null. The pedigree premium, as understood and applied by the PE industry, is a myth. The Fundamental Problem: Selection Effects Don't Transfer The pedigree hypothesis assumes that the selection effects of elite employers transfer to new contexts. If Goldman selects the top 1%, those individuals should remain the top 1% in any role. But this assumption fails because: Selection criteria are context-specific: Goldman selects for analytical horsepower, financial modeling skills, and tolerance for investment banking hours. McKinsey selects for structured problem-solving and client management. Google selects for engineering talent and innovation thinking. None of these selection criteria are the same as the criteria for PE-backed CEO success, which centers on operational leadership, board management, and execution under resource constraints. Performance is context-dependent: The same individual performs very differently in different organizational contexts. A brilliant Google VP may struggle to lead a $50M manufacturing company with outdated systems, union workforce, and PE board oversight. The within-person ICC of 6.82% from our analysis confirms this: even the SAME CEO gets different outcomes in different situations. Context dominates individual ability. Survivorship bias inflates pedigree: We observe FAANG, MBB, and elite banks as successful organizations and retroactively attribute their success to the quality of their people. But these organizations succeed primarily due to structural advantages: market position, network effects, brand, capital, and technology moats. The people in these organizations benefit from these structural advantages, not the other way around. What PE CEO Success Actually Requires PE-backed CEO roles demand a specific and unusual combination of capabilities that prestigious employers don't specifically develop: Operating with leverage: Managing a company under PE ownership means operating with significant debt service obligations, limited margin for error, and a board with specific return expectations on a defined timeline. This is fundamentally different from managing a division at Google or leading a consulting engagement. PE board relationships: The CEO-board dynamic in PE is uniquely intense. The CEO must manage board members who are also the company's owners, have deep financial expertise, and expect granular operational reporting. Success requires diplomatic skill, transparency, and the ability to manage up effectively. 100-day plan execution: PE ownership typically involves an aggressive value creation plan with specific milestones. CEOs must hit the ground running with operational improvements, talent upgrades, and strategic initiatives. The ramp-up period is measured in weeks, not quarters. Exit preparation: Unlike public company CEOs who manage for ongoing performance, PE-backed CEOs must manage toward an exit. This requires understanding buyer perspectives, preparing the business for due diligence, and building a narrative of value creation. The Path Forward: Relationship Intelligence Over Resume Screening If employer pedigree doesn't predict PE CEO success, what should firms screen for? Our research consistently points to contextual and relationship-based factors. Backchannel references provide information about how a candidate actually performs in relevant situations. Career overlap analysis reveals who has worked alongside the candidate and can provide candid assessments. Relationship mapping identifies the support networks that a CEO brings to the role. This is why tools like Verata's relationship intelligence platform represent a fundamental shift in how PE firms should approach talent decisions. Instead of filtering by brand name on a resume, firms can map the actual professional networks around a candidate, identify shared-tenure connections for backchannel diligence, and assess the relational context that our research shows matters far more than credentials. Altria’s Profile We have a leading portfolio of nicotine products for U.S. nicotine consumers age 21+. We are Moving Beyond Smoking® by responsibly transitioning adult smokers to a smoke-free future, competing vigorously for existing smoke-free adult nicotine consumers and exploring new growth opportunities — beyond the U.S. and beyond nicotine (Vision). To achieve our Vision, we will pursue initiatives designed to promote the long-term welfare of our company, our stakeholders, society at large and the environment. Our wholly owned subsidiaries include leading manufacturers of both combustible and smoke-free products. In combustibles, we own Philip Morris USA Inc. (PM USA), the most profitable U.S. cigarette manufacturer, and John Middleton Co. (Middleton), a leading U.S. cigar manufacturer. Our smoke-free portfolio includes ownership of U.S. Smokeless Tobacco Company LLC (USSTC), the leading global moist smokeless tobacco (MST) manufacturer, Helix Innovations LLC (Helix), a leading manufacturer of oral nicotine pouches, and NJOY, LLC (NJOY), an e-vapor manufacturer with products covered by marketing granted orders from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Additionally, we have a majority-owned joint venture, Horizon Innovations LLC (Horizon), for the U.S. marketing and commercialization of heated tobacco stick products. Our equity investments include Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV (ABI), the world’s largest brewer, and Cronos Group Inc. (Cronos), a leading Canadian cannabinoid company. The brand portfolios of our operating companies include Marlboro ®, Black & Mild ®, Copenhagen ®, Skoal ®, on! ® and NJOY ®. Trademarks related to Altria referenced in this release are the property of Altria or our subsidiaries or are used with permission. Learn more about Altria at www.altria.com and follow us on X, Facebook and LinkedIn. Basis of Presentation We report our financial results in accordance with GAAP. Our management reviews OCI, which is defined as operating income before general corporate expenses and amortization of intangibles, to evaluate the performance of, and allocate resources to, our segments. Our management also reviews certain financial results, including OCI, OCI margins and diluted EPS, on an adjusted basis, which excludes certain income and expense items, including those items noted under “2026 Full-Year Guidance.” Our management does not view any of these special items to be part of our underlying results as they may be highly variable, may be unusual or infrequent, are difficult to predict and can distort underlying business trends and results. Our management also reviews income tax rates on an adjusted basis. Our adjusted effective tax rate may exclude certain items from our reported effective tax rate. Our management believes that adjusted financial measures provide useful additional insight into underlying business trends and results, and provide a more meaningful comparison of year-over-year results. Our management uses adjusted financial measures for planning, forecasting and evaluating business and financial performance, including allocating capital and other resources and evaluating results relative to employee compensation targets. These adjusted financial measures are not required by, or calculated in accordance with, GAAP and may not be calculated the same as similarly titled measures used by other companies. These adjusted financial measures should thus be considered as supplemental in nature and not considered in isolation or as a substitute for the related financial information prepared in accordance with GAAP. We provide reconciliations of historical adjusted financial measures to corresponding GAAP measures in this release. We use the equity method of accounting for our investments in ABI and Cronos and report our share of ABI’s and Cronos’s results using a one-quarter lag because ABI’s and Cronos’s results are not available in time for us to record them in the concurrent period. The one-quarter reporting lag for ABI and Cronos does not affect our cash flows. Our reportable segments are (i) smokeable products, consisting of combustible cigarettes and machine-made large cigars, and (ii) oral tobacco products, consisting of MST and oral nicotine pouches. We have included results for NJOY, Horizon, Helix International and other business activities, which primarily consists of research and development expense related to certain new product platforms and technologies, in “All Other.” Comparisons are to the corresponding prior-year period unless otherwise stated. title: RMV Implements Further Extensions
summary: Safety Insurance is a premier provider of auto, home, and business owners insurance in Massachusetts, Maine, and New Hampshire.
body_text: Further Extensions Implemented for Expiring Licenses, Permits, Motor Vehicle Inspection Stickers, and Passenger Plate Registrations The Massachusetts RMV has implemented further extensions for expiring motor vehicle inspection stickers, passenger plate registrations, professional credentials, and licenses and permits, including Commercial Driver’s Licenses and Permits (CDLs / CLPs). While 60-day extensions had already been implemented for most credentials, passenger plate registrations, and inspection stickers expired or expiring in March and April, this new action will apply the same 60-day extension to those expiring in May. Additionally, credentials expiring in March 2020 that previously were extended by 60 days will have an additional 60-day extension applied. The following new changes are now effective: All commercial and non-commercial driver’s licenses, ID cards, and Learner’s Permits that expire in May 2020 will now expire in July 2020 and do not need to be renewed at this time. Customers holding a license marked “Limited-Term” that has expired or will expire between March 1 and May 31, 2020 should visit Mass.Gov/RMV for more information and to check the validity of their credential. The RMV also recently introduced an online renewal option for CDL holders if they are self-certified in the Non-Excepted Interstate (NI) category for medical certification. In accordance with updated guidance from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), all CDL Medical Certificates expiring between March 1 and April 30, 2020 will not expire until June 30, 2020 and do not need to be renewed at this time. Extensions to CDL Medical Certificates are intended to prevent license downgrades and elective medical visits, as well as alleviate demand on medical providers, during the State of Emergency. Motor vehicle safety and emissions inspection stickers that expire on May 31, 2020 will now expire on July 31, 2020. While automotive repair and maintenance facilities continue to remain open as “essential services” and inspection stations may operate at their discretion, these annual inspections do not need to occur at this time. All passenger plate registrations that will expire in May 2020, will now expire in July 2020. Registration renewals can continue to be performed online at Mass.Gov/RMV during this time. Customers seeking to do so in-person will not be able to make an appointment and should delay their visit to a Service Center at this time. Professional credentials for School Bus Certificates, School Pupil Transport Licenses (7D), Inspector Licenses, Inspection Station Licenses, Driving Instructor Licenses and Driving School Licenses that expire in May 2020 will be extended for 90 days after the State of Emergency is lifted and do not need to be renewed at this time. These additional extenstions under Governor Charlie Baker’s declaration of a State of Emergency on March 10 replicate the ongoing measures the RMV is taking to reduce the need for customers to physically visit an RMV Service Center or one of its business partners’ facilities, allowing for social distancing by decreasing non-essential travel and customer volume. Below is a summary of newly announced (in bold) and existing extensions. View details on all of these extensions and additional information on RMV services and the RMV’s response to COVID-19. Have Questions? Contact RMVATLASSupport@dot.state.ma.us . In this rapidly changing environment, please follow @MassRMV on Twitter to receive real-time updates to policy, services, and current Service Center status.

title: Why Packard Still Matters
summary: On a hill just behind The Lodge at Pebble Beach on California’s Monterey Peninsula, the world’s most exclusive traffic jam starts before sunrise every third Sunday in August. body_text: On a hill just behind The Lodge at Pebble Beach on California’s Monterey Peninsula, the world’s most exclusive traffic jam starts before sunrise every third Sunday in August. A queue of some 200 meticulously fettled machines sit bumper to bumper, waiting to roll onto a golf fairway and bask in the boundary where commerce and technology intersect with art. Among them in 2025 were 13 Packards, for the simple reason that there are always Packards on the lawn at Pebble Beach, because staging a Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance without a Packard is like staging King Lear without the king. Drive almost any antique car dating from the earliest years to about 1940 and, at some point, you are bound to be asked if it’s a Packard. Nearly 70 years after the brand disappeared from showrooms, it is the one name from the classic era that average people can recall at a moment’s notice. Packard’s fame lives on in old gangster movies, in stories that fathers and grandfathers tell at family gatherings about the cars they admired when they were kids, and in car shows where wide-eyed children gaze up at towering chrome grilles that seem to scrape the heavens, their parents unconsciously replanting the seed in the next generation by reading a placard and saying out loud, “Oh yeah, that’s a Packard.” Packard used several mascots over the decades, perhaps most famously the “chrome doughnut lady,” as some call the Goddess of Speed (top, left), a tribute to the Greek goddess Nike, which appeared in various forms on Packards from 1926 to 1950. Matt Tierney If there were a Mount Rushmore for cars, a Packard grille would be at top dead center. Fully a quarter-century into the 21st century, a Packard remains the bluest of blue-chip American classics, the quintessential car from the before times, the one that best epitomizes the elegance and formality of an earlier age and the old trope that “they sure don’t make ’em like they used to.” Machines bearing that famous script logo have roamed all the continents and defended democracy in the air and at sea. You don’t even have to ask the man who owns one, per the company’s famous ad tagline, because everyone already knows that Packard was the best America had to offer in a period when its empire was ascendant and its citizens seemed confident that it always would be. On a Mount Rushmore for cars, a Packard grille would be top dead center. “They were just a remarkably successful high-quality luxury firm in the era when a stand-alone luxury marque could survive,” affirms Chris Bock, chief judge at Pebble Beach and a strong advocate for keeping Packard as one of the first brands to be given a standing class at the event. That was in 1983, and more Packards have won Pebble’s coveted Best of Show award than any other brand except for Duesenberg. Says Bock, “I hear people saying, ‘Why would we celebrate Packard instead of Cadillac?’ and then I have to point out that there are more classic Packards extant than all the other luxury marques combined. They outsold most of the other marques from the classic era. It’s easy to defend.” “They used the best materials, they had the best craftsmen, Packard was the soft-spoken boss of the road,” said Ross Myers, a dairy farmer from Boyertown, Pennsylvania, who brought to Pebble a ’32 V-12 roadster. “I like fixing up stuff, and if you’re going to spend all the time to fix up an old car, I like it to be something special, and Packards to me are special.” “Everybody who is into classic cars wants a Packard,” said Stephen Babinsky of Automotive Restorations in Clinton Township, New Jersey. A serial Packard owner himself, he was on the lawn that morning overseeing the pre-judging prep of a dark blue Dietrich-body ’34 1107 Twelve Coupe restored in his shop. “Of course everybody wants a Duesenberg, too, but they are a different level. For somebody who wants to get into the hobby, Packards are the way to go because they’re really good cars and they’re affordable. They are just well engineered, and they’re good driving cars, especially the early ’30s stuff. I have Cadillacs, I have Chryslers, I have all kinds of sh*t, and the Packard is just the best all-around car.” Matt Tierney A new car bearing the Packard name hasn’t sold since 1958, yet the brand remains as relevant as Bentley, Bugatti, and Chevrolet in the hearts of collectors. What makes it so special has something to do with the magnificent cars and engines and a lot to do with the people behind them, most of whom didn’t bear the name Packard. In fact, Packard is further proof that men such as Henry Ford and Walter P. Chrysler, founders who remained with their companies long enough to see their names grow into carmaking institutions, are rarities in the annals of auto history. Louis Chevrolet lasted barely four years in his namesake startup before selling out, David Dunbar Buick just seven years. The engineering-minded James Ward Packard and his business-savvy brother William Doud Packard lasted only a decade in the car business before handing over the enterprise to others. Matt Tierney Descendants of early English colonial settlers, the thriving Packards of elysian, well-to-do Warren, Ohio, were already successful in various fields. The brothers ran a bustling factory producing incandescent lamps, wiring, and other electrical devices while their sister, Alaska Packard Davidson, was destined to become the first female investigator at the FBI (and one of the last until 1972, after being fired in 1924 by newly installed director J. Edgar Hoover). A trip to France in 1896 saw James Ward return with a de Dion-Bouton motorized tricycle, a stubborn and idiosyncratic device which seemed determined to uphold every crass French stereotype. Packard’s growing interest in cars undaunted, he then bought a car from Alexander Winton, his Scottish neighbor up the road in Cleveland. It proved to be hardly more reliable. According to Packard: A History of the Motor Car and the Company, by the editors of Automobile Quarterly , Packard made numerous trips back to the factory to get his motor carriage fixed and to suggest engineering changes. Finally, in 1899, in a scene that would play out again some 60 years later between Enzo Ferrari and Ferruccio Lamborghini, Winton exploded and told Packard that if he thought he could do better, he should damn well build his own car. Packard thought about it, then poached several of Winton’s key employees. His new auto firm, The New York and Ohio Company, produced its first car, the Model A, in November 1899 (the name was soon amended to The Ohio Automobile Company). A harbinger of future Packards and their renowned durability, that first car still exists, a gift from James Ward Packard to his alma mater, the engineering school at Lehigh University, which maintains it to this day in running condition. The new design featured a number of firsts for the auto industry. As a spark-fired internal combustion engine revs up, the timing of the spark needs to advance, and the standard practice into the 1920s was to affix a lever on the steering wheel that the driver could advance manually to keep the engine running properly. Being electrical men, the Packards endowed their car with automatic spark advance years before it became common. There was a rev limiter built into the distributor to prolong engine life. Orders began to trickle in as word got around town and the region. Legend has it that the company’s famous slogan, “Ask the man who owns one,” was born on a busy day in 1901 when the office secretary asked James Ward for a reply to a letter from a potential buyer in Pittsburgh inquiring about the car’s features. “Tell him I’ll be over to talk with him—no, wait, tell him to ask the man who owns one.” Right about so many things in 1899, by 1901, Packard was already falling out of step with the fast-moving industry. Yes, Packard was an early American adopter of the steering wheel to replace the tiller. The company also established the industry’s first training school for service mechanics. But the founder of the company that would later be famous for its V-12s believed that “more than one cylinder on a Packard would be like two tails on a cat—you just don’t need it.” James Ward held that a simple, reliable engine placed under the seat, which kept the weight centralized and low, with more of it on the rear axle for traction and stability, was better than putting a larger, more complex one under a removable cover out in front of the driver, as was rapidly becoming the industry standard. William Doud Packard pilots the company’s second car, the Model B, past the original plant in Warren, Ohio. Bettmann Archive/Getty Images Besides, James Ward and William Doud’s enthusiasm for the project seemed to be waning as their first interest, the growing electrical components business, demanded more of their attention. It’s thought that officially changing the name from the Ohio Automobile Company to the Packard Motor Car Company in late 1902 was an effort to make it easier to raise capital through share sales and, if necessary, move the operation out of state. No doubt they were influenced in part by the son of a prominent Detroit railroading family who had decided to become a major investor in Packard, the first of several outsiders who would build Packard into what it would become. Henry Joy’s arrival was the beginning of the end for Packard the carmaking brothers and the start of Packard the automobile institution. An ardent automobilist and fan of the product, Joy somehow convinced James Ward to hire a new chief engineer, Frenchman Charles Schmidt, who brought to the company fresh ideas already being tried in Europe. The proverbial two-tailed cat, the Packard Model G, arrived in 1902. Joy brought in other wealthy Detroit investors, and soon the rumor spread that the whole company would soon be decamping for the embryonic Motor City. By all accounts, Joy’s Detroit mob was amply funded and well organized, meaning Packard had a solid financial backing at a time when the industry was rife with penniless dreamers and honey-tongued charlatans. Joy had big ideas for Packard, the main one being the construction of an enormous new factory to replace the scattershot workshops in Warren where the cars had been built to that point. Given Joy’s ties to Detroit, a move was inevitable. Joy purchased the Weber farm, a 67-acre cow pasture at Grand Boulevard and Concord Avenue just northeast of what was then Detroit’s city limits, and hired the architect Albert Kahn, the already respected German immigrant whose industrial designs for Ford, Chrysler, and General Motors would become iconic. The newspapers estimated the new plant would increase the city’s labor pool by at least 1000 and drive up local property values. Joy figured his future king of car companies needed a suitably impressive castle. One early visitor to “the Boulevard,” as the new Packard headquarters came to be known, was no less than Henry Ford, whose own Packard limousine was stolen off the streets in Detroit in September 1916. The auto magnate went in person to retrieve the chassis and engine numbers in order to file a complete police report. “The Boulevard,” as insiders called Packard’s sprawling plant in Detroit. Universal Images Group/Getty Images Packard’s model designations by letter gave way to model designations by numerical series, a practice the company would use for decades, eschewing the more traditional use of model years that came with a relentless imperative for annual changes. The two-cylinder engines grew into four, then into six, then, in 1915, into the 12-cylinder Twin Six, the start of Packard’s long quest for the smoothest, most refined horsepower possible. “They didn’t get lost in the weeds trying to reinvent the wheel,” notes John Bothwell of Douglas and Company, a prewar specialist in Costa Mesa, California, who has worked on a number of Packards. “They stayed with conventional wisdom: When T-head engines were the thing, they had T-head engines, when everybody was doing twin-cylinder engines, that’s what they did. They weren’t trying to reengineer stuff, they just went with the trends, but they focused on doing what they did at a very high quality.” By 1912, a $6200 Packard limo was an avatar of American wealth. Universal Images Group/Getty Images The titular president of the company, James Ward had long since become a passenger on his own train, and in 1909, he and William Doud stepped back completely from the auto business. Henry Joy would soon be gone too, a victim of his boundless enthusiasm for distractions that the Packard board found exhausting. The search for the perfect man to run the enterprise took a year and ended when the next great figure in Packard’s history stepped into the story. Alvan Macauley—he hated when people misspelled it “Alvin”—was a 42-year-old patent lawyer from West Virginia who was already feted in Detroit’s industrial circles for reviving the fortunes of what would become the Burroughs Adding Machine Company. He did so in part with a lightning move of the factory and its 400 workers from St. Louis to Detroit that lost only two days of production. By 1916, Macauley was the president of Packard, a position he held along with chairman of the board for the next 32 years. The original garages at the Packard Proving Grounds Historic Site in Shelby Township, Michigan, are a perfect backdrop for an assortment of Packard’s elegant products. Opened in 1928 as the first of its type in the auto industry, the facility is now a 17-acre museum and event space. Matt Tierney The papers called him “tight-lipped and bespectacled,” and “the personification of conservatism.” It was said that he never lost his temper, that his favorite food was turtle soup, that he could both milk a cow and mill his own furniture, and that he hand-carved cigarette cases to give as gifts to friends. Besides a wood shop in which he spun out chairs and cabinets and miniature furniture for his grandchildren’s dolls, Macauley’s Grosse Pointe mansion contained rare tapestries, artwork by the great masters such as Rembrandt, and an enormous library. He could recite long literary passages from memory, and his favorite book was Lorna Doone , a 19th-century romance epic by the English author Richard Doddridge Blackmore. Which was slightly ironic since Macauley found long names annoying, a reason he dropped his own first name, James, to make his signature quicker to sign (a practice he encouraged in subordinates). His management philosophy was summed up by an inscription that hung for years in the Packard executive offices: “I know of no more stricture that can be passed upon the manager of any business than to have it said of him that in all his direction and handling of men, he developed mediocrities. We are on earth that we may ourselves succeed and enable others to succeed; the manager who develops among his organization the greatest number of successful men will himself enjoy the greatest measure of success.” Packard and Alvan Macauley are inextricably linked, Macauley having successfully helmed the company through the Great Depression and two world wars. He was the person the average Packard buyer wanted to be. Packard Proving Grounds Historic Site Urging Congress to lower tariffs just months before the Great Crash of 1929 got him on the July cover of Time magazine. In a rapidly growing Detroit that was a melting pot of immigrants, Macauley was an ardent America-firster, telling his shop-floor workers that advancement at Packard was dependent on learning English. They apparently revered him, partly because experienced craftsmen who grew too old to mill wood or machine metal were given easier jobs within the plant rather than turned out in the street. His stature among the rank and file climbed further when it was reported that his salary of $256,000 in 1929 was whittled down to $30,000 in the lean year of 1933. Unlike many of today’s executives, Macauley shared the pain when business was bad. Macauley was the embodiment of Packard’s customer. American newspapers helped make Macauley a household name by occasionally running his bylined column in which he opined on the economic and industrial issues of the day. His overriding message was one of optimism. Business was always looking up, from Macauley’s perspective, so long as men of good character were willing to do hard work. As chairman of the National Automobile Chamber of Commerce, one of several industry trade groups he chaired during his career, Macauley weighed in on everything from the shortage of parking spaces in Philadelphia to “the evils” of the trade-in scheme. Matt Tierney Contrary to his colleagues at other companies who were pioneering planned obsolescence with annual model changes, Macauley exhorted Packard owners never to trade in, but to keep their cars until they were entirely spent. Otherwise, he said, it only encouraged the industry to produce cheap, disposable cars, a waste of money and resources. “A homely but exact parallel might be found in a man at a fruit stand,” he wrote in a 1927 column that reads like one of Franklin Roosevelt’s folksy fireside chats. “A nickel for an apple, one bite, and then another apple might catch his eye because of a brighter color. One bite from that, after payment of another nickel, and then an unusual plumpness might intrigue him into the purchase of a third. “The remainders of the first two apples are as sound and just as good in every way as before the bites were taken, but they have been stigmatized and their value lowered because of use. They are used apples.” Macauley wondered that people who were so careful with their nickels by eating apples down to their core were nonetheless “prodigal with their hundreds of dollars” by trading in perfectly good automobiles. A 1925 Model 333 embodies a period when many of Packard’s rivals disappeared, unable to survive the era of the Model T and mass production. Matt Tierney Relentlessly upright, always immaculately dressed, a pillar in the business community, and apparently without vices, Macauley was the embodiment of Packard’s idealized customer. While the Hollywood glitterati bought Packards clothed in flamboyant bespoke coachwork by Dietrich, Murphy, or Hibbard & Darrin, many ordinary bankers and businessmen bought Standard Eights because they thought they were—or wanted to be—Alvan Macauley. And in the next great figure in Packard history, chief engineer Jesse Gurney Vincent, whom Macauley brought over from Burroughs in 1912, the company had the man to create the cars to fit the image. Matt Tierney An Arkansan who dropped out of school in the eighth grade to work as a blacksmith and a machinist, Vincent would eventually attach his name to more than 400 patents. He wasn’t at Packard long before drafting a 35-page memo outlining the advantages of a V-12 engine. “From the time when the first practical car made its first run on the road,” Vincent summed up, “there have been three things which every motorist asked for—more range of ability, greater smoothness, and less noise.” These attributes came to define Packard’s guiding principles through its golden years of the ’20s and ’30s. Though Vincent would be associated with the development of four-wheel and power brakes, air conditioning, and hypoid gears, as well as one of the industry’s first vehicle proving grounds, his first love was engines. Anchoring the company’s reputation as the “Master Motor Builders” were perfectly balanced straight-sixes and -eights and whispering V-12s with hydraulic valve-lash adjusters for ultimate silence. An avid pilot, Vincent was a co-architect of Packard’s World War I mainstay, the light but powerful Liberty aircraft engine (an effort that earned him the rank of colonel in the U.S. Army Signal Corps). With Macauley’s enthusiastic support, he also developed the first diesel aircraft engine. And he worked with champion boat racer Gar Wood to stuff multiple Liberty engines into racing hulls in the 1920s, an effort that directly led to the company’s marine engine business. The 1942 Model 2021 was Packard’s last expression of elegance before the war. Matt Tierney With the next war looming, Packard accepted the enormous job of building the Rolls-Royce Merlin aircraft engine under license after Ford passed on the contract, judging the hand-built 27-liter V-12 to be “unsuitable for mass production.” Vincent wrote one of his legendary memos, enthusiastically endorsing the project and figuring the company would need a separate plant employing 14,000 workers to fulfill a wartime demand that would see more than 55,000 Packard-Merlins produced. Delicate negotiations with the protective British over the design dragged out for months, their armed services demanding features in which the U.S. War Department had no interest. Everything from thread pitches to block castings to carburetor types to supercharger configurations were points of contention. While Packard didn’t completely redesign the Merlin, it made so many changes that its version resembled the original about as much as a Tennessee twang resembled a Liverpool scouse. The same mother tongue, but that’s about it. Chief engineer Jesse Gurney Vincent was interested in boat racing, which led directly to Packard building huge marine engines. Examples of Packard cars and engines can be seen at the Packard Proving Grounds Historic Site in Michigan. Matt Tierney At the same time, Packard cranked out thousands of the 4M 2500, a 2490-cubic-inch, 1200-hp V-12 marine leviathan. Three of these engines in the 80-foot Elco PT-109 propelled a young Lieutenant (JG) John F. Kennedy and his crew to almost 50 mph while patrolling the Solomon Islands. Over in Europe, General Dwight D. Eisenhower shuttled to and from his headquarters in an army green Packard sedan, and Joseph Stalin was such a fan that he ordered his own domestic limo maker, ZiL, to exactly copy Packard’s designs. Knockoff Packards built by ZiL and, later, GAZ, ferried the party elite in the Soviet Union for decades. Packard cranked out thousands of the 1200-hp V-12s. After the war, forces that had been pushing Packard to lower the drawbridge with less expensive cars gained momentum. The introduction of the “junior” Packards of 1937, with prices starting at $795, an unfathomably low sum for a new Packard, led to the Boulevard’s best sales year ever: 109,518 cars. The success of the juniors caused Packard to rethink its antiquated and somewhat artisanal production methods and embrace mass manufacturing techniques that lowered costs. These changes served Packard for a time when the peace came. However, some bad product decisions, waves of labor strikes, and postwar shortages and inflation started Packard’s long slide toward its disastrous 1954 merger with Studebaker. While new Clippers and Caribbeans remained status symbols in the nicer parts of town, Packard, the independent luxury automaker, could not compete against the Cadillacs, Lincolns, and Chryslers that had huge manufacturing and sales organizations powered by the million-unit sales of mass-market brands to sustain them. It hung on much longer than its brothers in the once-formidable “Three P’s” (Packard, Peerless, and Pierce-Arrow), but eventually time and progress caught up to Packard with an anticlimactic decision in 1958 by the Studebaker-Packard Corp. to drop the Packard name altogether. When asked, owners and restorers are hard-pressed to come up with specifics as to what made Packards stand above. “They just drive a little easier, the brakes are a little better, the shifting is easier, the machine work is a little tighter,” said Babinsky, the New Jersey restorer, before admitting, “Honestly, I don’t know what the combination is.” Packard was the last independent American luxury manufacturer when it merged with Studebaker in 1954, having outlasted its peers and outsold for years even well-funded rivals such as Cadillac and Lincoln, which were just luxury divisions of much larger automakers. Matt Tierney Owners of cars from this era talk a lot about how Packard used solid brass and bronze in their door handles and other fittings, whereas other luxury brands used cheaper pot metal, a metal alloy of various low-cost materials such as zinc, lead, and copper that is cooked up in a “pot.” It’s a reputation for quality “that has never gone away,” said Craig Handley, president of the marque’s oldest national owner organization, the 73-year-old Packard Club. “What attracts people still, after all these years, is that reputation. All the histories of the industry portray Packard as the Rolls-Royce of America, that it was the ultimate car.” They just drive a little easier, the brakes are a little better, the machine work is a little tighter. Ultimately, what keeps Packard relevant is its story as much as the machines. They say that nothing lasts forever, and to be sure, Packard’s full run was a mere 59 years, meaning it has been gone longer than it was alive. But if you’re wondering how it’s possible that old guys who were excited about Packards in the 1960s got replaced by new old guys who were excited about Packards in the 1980s, and how that cycle keeps repeating to this day (such that the Pebble Beach Concours today still receives far more Packard applications than it can accept), then consider that the story of one of America’s great car companies still fascinates us. It still inspires people to keep retelling it and to keep sinking their time and money into preserving the cars. And it’s looking like it always will. title: Weekly Market Update – July 20, 2026 · Inter&Co Blog
summary: U.S. equities ended a volatile week lower as tech stocks declined, inflation data eased rate concerns, oil surged, and Big Tech earnings moved into focus.
body_text: A volatile and negative week for US equities, with tech leading the losses. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, the S&P 500 declined 1.6%, and the Dow Jones showed greater resilience with a 0.9% drop. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell as much as 20% for the month, as the market questioned whether AI investments will translate into near-term earnings. Chinese competition further unsettled investors, with the launch of Moonshot AI's new model catching the market off guard. On the positive side, Q2 earnings season kicked off on solid footing, with major US banks delivering strong results. On the macro and fixed income front, the latest inflation data brought some relief. A cooler-than-expected CPI print reduced bets on further Fed rate hikes, with the market now pricing approximately 45bps of additional tightening through 2027. Nevertheless, the 10-year Treasury yield rose 5bps as geopolitical risks resurfaced, with the US-Iran conflict escalating and reducing the chances of a positive ceasefire outcome. Brent crude surged 15% on the week, topping USD 85 per barrel. Looking ahead, the market turns its attention to hyperscaler earnings — Google this week, followed by Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon the week after — as the key catalyst for equities, with a sharp focus on AI monetization and future capex intentions. Big Tech results will be an important test for whether the recent tech selloff represents a healthy correction or the beginning of a more structural reversal.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Chargeback Win Rate: Calculation, Improvement & Benchmarks
summary: Master your chargeback win rate. Learn to calculate, analyze, and significantly improve your success against disputes with Dispute Ninja's expert guide for merchants.
body_text: Are you leaving money on the table due to unresolved chargebacks? Many merchants are, often because they haven't optimized their chargeback win rate. This critical metric directly impacts your profitability and operational health, yet it's frequently overlooked or misunderstood. A low chargeback win rate doesn't just mean lost revenue from individual disputes; it signals deeper issues in your fraud prevention and representment processes. This comprehensive guide will demystify the chargeback win rate, teach you how to accurately calculate it, provide industry benchmarks, and equip you with actionable strategies to significantly improve your chargeback win rate, turning disputes into successful recoveries. By understanding and optimizing this key metric, you can protect your revenue and strengthen your business operations. Understanding Your Chargeback Win Rate Your chargeback win rate is more than just a number; it's a direct indicator of your business's ability to successfully recover revenue from disputed transactions. For any merchant processing online payments, understanding this metric is fundamental to financial health and operational efficiency. It provides insight into the effectiveness of your dispute resolution strategies. This section lays the groundwork, defining what the chargeback win rate truly represents and why it holds such significant importance for your business. We will explore its definition, why it matters, and how it differs from other related metrics. What is a Chargeback Win Rate? The chargeback win rate is the percentage of chargeback disputes that a merchant successfully overturns in their favor. Essentially, it measures your success in reclaiming funds that customers have disputed. A higher dispute success rate means you are more effective at proving the legitimacy of a transaction and recovering revenue. This metric is crucial for evaluating the performance of your chargeback management efforts. It directly reflects your ability to present compelling evidence and navigate the complex rules set by card networks. Optimizing your merchant dispute success rate can significantly impact your bottom line. Why Does Your Win Rate Matter? Your chargeback win rate directly correlates with your business's financial stability and operational costs. A high win rate means more revenue recovered, less profit erosion, and a stronger defense against various forms of fraud, including friendly fraud. It demonstrates that your representment process is robust and effective. Beyond immediate financial recovery, a strong chargeback win rate also signals effective fraud prevention and customer service practices. It helps identify vulnerabilities in your transaction processes and allows for continuous improvement. Ultimately, a good win rate contributes to overall operational efficiency and protects your hard-earned revenue. How to Calculate Your Chargeback Win Rate Accurately Accurately calculating your chargeback win rate is the first step toward understanding and improving it. Without precise data, any strategies you implement will be based on guesswork. This section provides a straightforward guide to the formula and the essential data points required for precise tracking. Understanding how to calculate chargeback win rate will empower you to monitor your performance and make data-driven decisions. We will also discuss common calculation pitfalls to ensure your figures are reliable. The Standard Win Rate Formula The chargeback win rate calculation is straightforward. It's determined by dividing the number of disputes you won by the total number of disputes you responded to, then multiplying by 100 to get a percentage. This provides your win rate percentage against all cases where you attempted representment. The formula is: (Number of Won Disputes / Total Number of Represented Disputes) \* 100 = Chargeback Win Rate % For example, if you won 25 out of 50 disputes you responded to, your chargeback win rate would be (25 / 50) \* 100 = 50%. This simple formula provides a clear metric for your success. Data Points You Need for Accurate Tracking To accurately calculate chargeback win rate, you need precise chargeback data tracking for every dispute. Key data points include the total number of chargebacks received, how many you decided to represent, the number of disputes you won, and the number you lost. It’s also helpful to track disputes that were withdrawn by the cardholder. This data is typically found within your payment gateway's dashboard, through your acquirer, or via specialized chargeback management software. Consistent and meticulous tracking of these dispute outcomes is essential for reliable win rate analysis. Without this granular data, your win rate calculations may be misleading. What's a Good Chargeback Win Rate? Industry Benchmarks & Factors Understanding your chargeback win rate is important, but knowing what constitutes a" good" rate provides crucial context. Industry benchmarks can offer a general idea, but what's considered a strong average chargeback win rate can vary significantly. This section explores typical ranges and the various factors affecting chargeback win rate. Setting realistic goals for your business requires understanding these nuances. We will delve into industry averages and the key elements that influence your specific win rate performance. Understanding Industry Averages While there's no universally "perfect" chargeback win rate, industry ranges typically fall between 40% and 60%. However, these industry chargeback win rates are broad averages and can be misleading. Factors like your specific industry, the types of products or services you sell, and your transaction volume can all influence what a realistic benchmark looks like. For instance, high-risk industries or businesses with a higher volume of digital goods might naturally have lower win rates than those selling physical products with clear delivery confirmations. It's crucial to use benchmark comparison as a guide, not a rigid target, and to focus on continuous improvement specific to your business model. Key Factors Influencing Your Win Rate Numerous elements contribute to your chargeback win rate, explaining why some merchants experience a low win rate. The quality and relevance of your evidence quality are paramount; weak or incomplete documentation is a primary reason for dispute losses. The specific chargeback type impact also plays a significant role, as some reason codes are inherently harder to dispute (e.g., true fraud vs. friendly fraud). Internal factors like your representment process efficiency and your team's expertise are critical. External factors, such as the specific card network rules (Visa, Mastercard, etc.) and the overall regulatory environment, also influence outcomes. Our clients often find that even experienced merchants can overlook critical details when managing a high volume of disputes, leading to avoidable losses. Strategic Approaches to Significantly Improve Your Chargeback Win Rate Improving your chargeback win rate requires a multi-faceted approach that spans prevention, representment, and post-dispute analysis. It’s not just about winning individual cases but building a resilient system. This section outlines strategies to increase chargeback win rate that are both actionable and sustainable. By implementing these effective chargeback management techniques, you can move toward winning chargeback cases more consistently. We will cover steps you can take before, during, and after a dispute to optimize your success. Proactive Prevention: Before the Dispute The best way to improve your chargeback win rate is to prevent chargebacks from occurring in the first place. Robust chargeback prevention starts with clear communication. Ensure your billing descriptors are recognizable, so customers immediately identify transactions on their statements. Implementing fraud detection tools that screen for suspicious activity at the point of sale can drastically reduce fraudulent transactions. Excellent customer service best practices are also vital. Promptly addressing customer inquiries, offering easy refunds, and transparent policies can resolve issues before they escalate into disputes. Mastering Representment: Building a Winning Case Once a chargeback is initiated, your ability to master chargeback representment tips becomes critical. Timely responses are non-negotiable; adhere strictly to all dispute response deadlines set by card networks. Each case requires a tailored, well-structured response, not a generic template. The cornerstone of a strong representment package is compelling evidence. This evidence can include transaction details, customer communication logs, delivery confirmations, IP addresses, and proof of prior purchases. Organize your evidence clearly, cross-reference it with the chargeback reason code, and present it concisely to the card issuer. For an in-depth resource, consult our chargeback representment guide . Post-Dispute Analysis: Learning from Losses Even with the best strategies, you won't win every dispute. The key is to view losses as learning opportunities for future chargeback analysis. Regularly reviewing lost cases helps identify patterns and weaknesses in your processes. Was the evidence insufficient? Was a deadline missed? Was the chargeback reason code particularly challenging? This analysis is crucial for identifying win rate patterns and refining your strategies. Use dispute feedback from card networks or your chargeback management provider to understand where your case fell short. By continuously learning from past outcomes, you can implement targeted improvements and significantly boost your future chargeback win rate. Common Pitfalls That Lower Chargeback Win Rates Even experienced merchants can fall prey to common mistakes that severely impact their chargeback win rate. Identifying and avoiding these pitfalls is just as important as implementing winning strategies. Understanding the reasons for low chargeback win rate can save you significant time and resources. This section highlights the most frequent errors in chargeback management and provides actionable advice on avoiding dispute losses. We will also briefly touch upon how different chargeback codes require tailored responses. Top Mistakes in Chargeback Management One of the most frequent chargeback errors is submitting insufficient or irrelevant evidence. A generic response that doesn't directly address the chargeback reason code significantly reduces your chances of winning. Another critical mistake is missing the strict representment deadlines; a late submission is an automatic loss, regardless of your evidence. Poor record-keeping leads to evidence gaps, making it nearly impossible to build a strong case. Additionally, failing to understand the specific rules and requirements of each card network for different chargeback types can lead to avoidable losses. Each of these errors contributes directly to a lower chargeback win rate. Overcoming Challenges with Specific Chargeback Codes Different chargeback codes require highly tailored responses, and a one-size-fits-all approach is a common pitfall. For example, a"merchandise not received"dispute (e.g., Visa Reason Code 10.4) demands proof of delivery, while a"fraud"dispute (e.g., Mastercard Reason Code 4837) requires transaction data, IP addresses, and potentially previous purchase history. Attempting to use the same evidence for different codes will often result in a loss. Understanding these nuances is vital for improving your chargeback win rate. For a comprehensive overview of how to tackle various dispute types, explore our guide on[common chargeback codes](INTERNAL-LINK-PLACEHOLDER: /common-chargeback-codes). Leveraging Technology for Higher Chargeback Win Rates In today's fast-paced e-commerce environment, manual chargeback management can be overwhelming and inefficient. Leveraging technology is no longer a luxury but a necessity for achieving a higher chargeback win rate. Specialized chargeback management software can automate many tedious processes, significantly improving your efficiency and success. This section explores how automation and advanced analytics can transform your dispute resolution process. It highlights how technology can streamline your efforts and provide data-driven insights for continuous improvement. Automating Evidence Collection & Submission One of the most time-consuming aspects of chargeback representment is gathering and formatting compelling evidence. Automated chargeback responses streamline this process by integrating with your payment gateway, CRM, and shipping providers to automatically pull relevant transaction data. This ensures all required documents are collected quickly and accurately. This automation not only reduces manual effort but also minimizes the risk of human error and missed deadlines. By enabling a more efficient dispute process, technology ensures that your responses are always robust and timely, directly contributing to a higher chargeback win rate. Data-Driven Insights for Continuous Improvement Beyond automation, chargeback management platforms offer powerful chargeback analytics. These tools provide in-depth reporting on your chargeback win rate performance, identifying trends, common chargeback reasons, and areas for improvement. You can track your success rates by product, customer segment, or chargeback reason code. These win rate optimization tools help you understand *why* you're winning or losing disputes, enabling you to refine your prevention and representment strategies. We've observed that businesses utilizing automated solutions gain a significant competitive edge by turning raw data into actionable insights for continuous improvement. Conclusion Mastering your chargeback win rate is not merely about recovering lost funds; it's about building a robust, resilient business capable of navigating the complexities of modern commerce. By accurately calculating this metric, understanding industry benchmarks, and implementing strategic prevention and representment tactics, you gain a powerful lever for protecting your revenue and enhancing operational efficiency. The path to a higher chargeback win rate involves meticulous data tracking, compelling evidence, timely responses, and continuous learning from every dispute. Leveraging technology can significantly streamline these efforts, turning potential losses into successful recoveries. Take control of your chargeback win rate today, and transform your approach from reactive to proactive. Ready to take control of your chargebacks and significantly improve your chargeback win rate ? Explore Dispute Ninja's advanced solutions and discover how our platform can automate your representment process, provide data-driven insights, and help you recover more revenue.
