title: Everything You Need to Know About Construction Management
summary: If you're new to construction management, this is everything you need to know to become a pro.
body_text: Modern challenges reshaping construction management Today's construction managers operate in an environment fundamentally different from even five years ago. Labor availability has become a critical bottleneck in many markets, with experienced tradespeople retiring faster than new workers enter the field. Simultaneously, material costs have become less predictable, supply chain disruptions can emerge with little warning, and the regulatory landscape continues to expand with requirements around sustainability, accessibility, and environmental compliance. Beyond these external pressures, construction managers must navigate an increasingly complex client landscape. Modern project owners are more sophisticated, more informed through digital channels, and demand greater transparency throughout the construction process. They expect real-time visibility into project status, cost tracking, and quality metrics. This shift has elevated construction management from a tactical role focused on execution to a strategic function that requires strong business acumen alongside construction knowledge. Adding to this complexity, most construction projects now involve multiple approval bodies—local government agencies, utility companies, environmental regulators, and sometimes neighborhood groups. Managing these relationships while keeping projects moving forward requires political awareness, patience, and strategic communication that extends far beyond traditional construction expertise. Combating scope creep and change management One of the most insidious threats to project success isn't dramatic failure—it's gradual erosion through scope creep. Small requests that seem harmless accumulate into substantial cost and schedule impacts. A client asks for slightly better finishes. The architect suggests a minor reconfiguration that could improve functionality. A subcontractor identifies an efficiency opportunity that requires a slight design modification. Each change individually seems reasonable, but collectively they can consume project margins and consume schedules. Effective construction management requires a disciplined change control process that treats every modification seriously. This means establishing a clear baseline definition of project scope that all parties understand and accept. It means implementing a formal change order process where every modification is documented, costed, and explicitly approved before work begins. It means training project teams to recognize when scope is being modified informally and to flag these issues immediately. The most successful construction managers implement visual scope management tools—detailed drawings, 3D models, and specification documents that are referenced throughout the project. When scope questions arise, the conversation is grounded in what was contractually agreed upon, not what stakeholders remember discussing months earlier. This removes emotion from the discussion and creates a shared reference point for all parties. Technology's role in modern construction oversight Construction has historically been one of the slower industries to adopt technology, but this is rapidly changing. Modern construction management increasingly relies on digital tools that provide visibility and control impossible to achieve through traditional methods. Building Information Modeling (BIM) has revolutionized how construction managers coordinate complex projects. Rather than working from 2D drawings that may contain conflicts, teams work with 3D digital models that integrate structural, mechanical, electrical, and architectural systems. Clash detection tools identify conflicts before they reach the jobsite, preventing costly rework. Models can be updated throughout construction to reflect actual conditions, creating as-built documentation that serves as a valuable operations reference for the owner. Real-time jobsite tracking technology provides unprecedented visibility into project progress. Automated progress photography, drone-based site monitoring, and sensor networks can track material movement, equipment utilization, and labor productivity with minimal manual effort. Construction managers can identify inefficiencies and bottlenecks as they occur, rather than discovering them in end-of-week reports. Integrated project management platforms now consolidate scheduling, budgeting, quality tracking, and communication into single systems accessible to all stakeholders. Rather than managing fragmented spreadsheets and email threads, project managers work from unified data sources where information is current and accessible from mobile devices on the jobsite. However, technology is a tool, not a solution. Construction managers who embrace technology effectively combine digital insights with human judgment, experience, and relationship-building skills. The most successful managers use technology to amplify their effectiveness, not replace their decision-making. Managing competing stakeholder interests Every construction project involves multiple parties with different priorities and success metrics. The project owner wants quality and value. The contractor wants profitable execution. Subcontractors want predictable work flow and prompt payment. The general public may want minimal traffic disruption. Regulators want code compliance. These interests don't always align, and construction managers must navigate these tensions carefully. This requires what might be called "stakeholder translation"—understanding what each party genuinely needs and finding ways to meet those needs without sacrificing other project objectives. Sometimes this means exploring creative solutions that give stakeholders what they actually want, even if it looks different from what they initially requested. For example, when a homeowner requests expanded scope late in a residential project, rather than immediately saying yes or no, an experienced construction manager might dig deeper. What problem is the owner trying to solve? Is there a way to address that problem within the current budget and schedule? Can work be staged differently? Are there alternative materials or approaches that meet the owner's underlying need at a lower cost? This consultative approach often leads to better outcomes than a transactional change order process. Regular stakeholder meetings are essential, but how these meetings are structured matters enormously. Effective construction managers prepare agendas that mix reporting on achievements with collaborative problem-solving for challenges. They present information visually rather than through lengthy verbal recitations. They make meetings forward-focused rather than blame-focused when issues arise. These practices build trust and create genuine partnerships rather than adversarial relationships. Building realistic contingency planning Many construction managers treat contingency budgets as slack to be eliminated through efficiency rather than as essential project reserves. This approach inevitably leads to either cost overruns or scope reduction when unforeseen conditions emerge—and they always do. Sophisticated contingency planning begins with a detailed risk assessment that identifies specific potential problems: soil conditions that might differ from subsurface investigation, weather events that could delay exterior work, supply chain disruptions, labor availability challenges, or regulatory requirement changes. Rather than a single percentage contingency applied uniformly across the project, this approach allocates specific reserves against identified risks. As projects progress and risk becomes clearer, contingency allocation changes. Early in a project, contingency might be higher because so much remains unknown. As site conditions are revealed and material orders are placed, certain risks are retired and contingency can be reduced. This dynamic approach provides more accuracy and better reflects actual project conditions than static contingency calculations. The key is distinguishing between genuine contingency for unexpected conditions and inefficient execution. Contingency should absorb true surprises, not poor planning. Construction managers must ensure their base plans are realistic and their contingencies are genuinely reserved for unknowns, not used as a crutch for inadequate planning. Subcontractor performance and accountability On most commercial and institutional projects, the general contractor oversees dozens of subcontractors, each responsible for specialized portions of work. The general contractor doesn't build the building—subcontractors do. Therefore, construction management is largely about managing subcontractor performance, which is considerably more complex than simply directing your own employees. Effective subcontractor management begins before they're selected. Clear bid documents that establish expectations around quality, schedule, safety, and reporting create a foundation for successful relationships. Thorough contractor qualification reviews assess not just price, but experience, financial stability, safety record, and capacity to deliver. Selecting the lowest bidder often leads to problems; selecting partners who can genuinely deliver the work at the bid price provides better value. Once subcontractors are mobilized, consistent oversight ensures they understand expectations and maintain performance. This isn't about micromanagement but about clear communication of requirements and accountability when performance falls short. Regular meetings with subcontractors ensure they understand schedule sequencing, quality standards, and coordination requirements. Daily jobsite presence allows managers to catch issues early when corrections are still possible. Payment serves as a powerful management tool. Connecting payment to verified completion of contractual obligations creates incentive alignment. Withholding payment when work doesn't meet standards until corrections are completed demonstrates that accountability is genuine, not theoretical. This requires discipline to maintain payment schedules for performing contractors while holding others accountable, but it's essential for managing a multi-party project. Integrating sustainability into project delivery Sustainability requirements have shifted from nice-to-have aspirations to contractual obligations on most projects. Whether pursuing formal certification like LEED, Net Zero, or Passivhaus, or simply meeting increasing owner and regulatory expectations, construction managers must incorporate sustainability from the planning phase through completion. This affects multiple aspects of construction management. Material sourcing becomes more complex when projects require recycled content, local sourcing, or low-carbon alternatives. Waste management requires more than dumpsters—careful sorting and tracking of recycled materials. Energy performance testing during construction may reveal issues requiring immediate correction. Construction practices that minimize environmental impact—dust control, water management, wildlife protection—require different procedures than conventional approaches. Successful integration of sustainability requires viewing it not as an additional burden but as an opportunity to demonstrate innovation and reduce lifecycle costs. A material choice that costs slightly more upfront but provides superior durability and lower maintenance costs over the building's lifespan is a smart business decision, not a sustainability sacrifice. Construction managers who understand this frame can often find sustainability approaches that improve both environmental performance and project economics. Data-driven decision making and predictive analytics Traditional construction management relied heavily on experience and intuition. Modern management increasingly incorporates data analysis and predictive modeling to support decision-making. Schedule analytics can identify which activities pose the greatest risk to project completion, allowing managers to focus attention on critical bottlenecks rather than spreading effort uniformly. Cost analytics can benchmark labor productivity against historical data or industry standards, identifying when crews are underperforming and investigating root causes. Quality metrics can track defect trends, identifying whether quality is improving or degrading, and pinpointing which subcontractors or work areas need additional attention. Predictive analytics go further, using historical data to forecast future conditions. Weather data combined with schedule information can predict the probability of weather delays and suggest optimal activity sequencing. Labor productivity curves can forecast completion timelines based on current crew performance. Material price trends can identify optimal procurement timing. These tools don't replace human judgment but inform it with better data. The challenge for construction managers is distinguishing between data that's genuinely actionable and data that creates false precision. Not everything that can be measured matters. Construction managers must maintain healthy skepticism about metrics while remaining open to insights that data reveals. The goal is informed intuition, not data-driven decision-making that ignores contextual factors. Building a collaborative project culture Construction projects that succeed despite challenging conditions often share a distinctive characteristic: a collaborative culture where all parties work toward common objectives rather than protecting narrow interests. Building this culture is a responsibility of construction management. Culture starts with leadership modeling. When the construction manager treats subcontractors as partners rather than adversaries, establishes shared success metrics, and works creatively to solve problems rather than assign blame, others follow that example. Regular team meetings that celebrate achievements build esprit de corps. Recognizing individual and team contributions, publicly acknowledging good work, and creating opportunities for workers to contribute ideas to problem-solving build engagement. Collaborative culture requires creating psychological safety—an environment where people can voice concerns, ask questions, and suggest improvements without fear of punishment. Many construction jobsites operate under command-and-control hierarchies where workers follow orders without question. More sophisticated projects recognize that frontline workers often see problems before management does. Creating channels for that information to surface and creating processes to act on legitimate concerns improves both safety and efficiency. Safety culture deserves special mention because it's where collaborative culture has the most tangible impact. When all participants share responsibility for safety, when near-misses are reported and investigated rather than hidden, when workers feel empowered to stop work that's unsafe, safety performance improves. Conversely, when safety is perceived as the safety manager's responsibility rather than everyone's responsibility, safety performance suffers. Measuring construction management success How construction management is measured shapes what gets prioritized. Many construction organizations measure success primarily by cost performance—did we stay within budget? This creates incentive to control costs above all else, which can lead to cutting corners on quality or safety. A more balanced approach measures success across multiple dimensions. Schedule performance indicates whether the project will be completed when promised. Missing schedule targets has costs that extend beyond the construction contract—delayed building openings lose revenue, extended construction overhead consumes profits, and broken promises damage client relationships. Quality performance should be measured not just during construction but post-occupancy. Defect rates, warranty claim frequency, and owner satisfaction provide better measures of true quality than punch-list completion rates. Some of the best predictors of long-term project reputation are owner satisfaction surveys conducted months or years after project completion. Safety performance is often measured by incident rates, but leading indicators like near-miss reporting and safety audit findings provide earlier warning of cultural issues. Projects with strong safety cultures typically show this in lower incident rates, but the culture itself is the real measure. Financial performance matters, but should be measured as actual profitability versus planned profitability, not just cost control. A project that comes in under budget but doesn't generate planned margins due to inefficient execution is not successful. Similarly, a project that generates planned margins only because change orders consumed contingency and created cost overruns for the client isn't a sustainable success model. Relationship quality often gets overlooked but predicts future business success. Clients satisfied enough to hire the same contractor for future projects, subcontractors eager to work on future projects, and employees who recommend the company to others indicate that projects were managed not just competently but positively. The future of construction management Construction management will continue to evolve as the industry faces increasing pressure to build more quickly, sustainably, and affordably. Several trends are likely to reshape the discipline in coming years. Modular and prefabricated construction will shift more work off-site, changing how construction management operates. Rather than coordinating diverse trades on a construction site, managers will increasingly oversee factory production and assembly of pre-built modules, with on-site work focused on integration and finishing. Robotics and automation will handle more routine tasks, reducing labor dependency and changing how crew productivity is managed. Rather than managing crews performing manual tasks, construction managers will increasingly manage mixed human-and-automated work teams. Integrated project delivery models like design-build and construction management-at-risk align incentives across the project team. These delivery methods will likely expand as owners recognize the risk reduction and improved outcomes compared to traditional design-bid-build approaches. This requires construction managers to think differently about their role, shifting from adversarial cost control to collaborative value optimization. Workforce development will become increasingly critical as labor shortages persist. Construction firms that excel at training, mentoring, and retaining skilled workers will have competitive advantages. Construction management will expand to include responsibility for workforce planning and development, not just task execution. Through all these changes, the fundamental responsibility of construction management remains: delivering projects that meet owner needs at the planned cost and schedule while maintaining safety and quality standards. The tools and techniques will continue to evolve, but the discipline of disciplined planning, disciplined oversight, and disciplined adaptation will remain essential. ‍

body_text: PDF Version SHANGHAI, July 02, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Jiayin Group Inc. (“Jiayin” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: JFIN), a leading fintech platform in China, today announced that Ms. Xiaojing Lu has been appointed as a director of the Company’s board of directors (the “Board”), a member of the compensation committee of the Board and a member of the nominating and corporate governance committee of the Board, effective as of July 1, 2026. Ms. Yifang Xu has resigned from her position as a director of the Company, a member of the compensation committee of the Board and a member of the nominating and corporate governance committee of the Board, effective as of July 1, 2026, for personal reasons. Ms. Xiaojing Lu brings over 15 years of expertise in financial technology and services to the Board, with a proven track record spanning credit user growth, credit operations, and risk management. Ms. Lu has served as Vice President of Credit User Growth Operations since April 2025, spearheading the Company’s borrower acquisition, lifecycle engagement, and operational initiatives. Since joining the Company in 2019, she has been responsible for market expansion, operational scaling, and risk strategy, having previously served as Senior Director and Director of Credit User Growth Operations from 2021 to April 2025, and Senior Manager of Risk Strategy from 2019 to 2021. Prior to joining the Company, Ms. Lu led risk management and credit operations teams at various financial information services firms from 2015 to 2019. She began her career at Ping An Data Technology (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. in 2011. Ms. Lu is currently pursuing an Executive MBA at China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) and she received her MBA from East China Normal University in 2023. Mr. Dinggui Yan, the Company’s Founder, Director and Chief Executive Officer, commented, “On behalf of the Board and the company, I would like to express our sincere gratitude to Ms. Yifang Xu for her dedicated service and valued insights during her tenure as director. We are pleased to appoint Ms. Xiaojing Lu as a director. Over the past six years, Ms. Lu has been a vital leader within our executive team, demonstrating a profound understanding of our operational framework and industry ecosystem. Her proven leadership and deep corporate insight will be invaluable to the sustainable development of the Company.” About Jiayin Group Inc. Jiayin Group Inc. is a leading fintech platform in China committed to facilitating effective, transparent, secure and fast connections between underserved individual borrowers and financial institutions. The origin of the business of the Company can be traced back to 2011. The Company operates a highly secure and open platform with a comprehensive risk management system and a proprietary and effective risk assessment model which employs advanced big data analytics and sophisticated algorithms to accurately assess the risk profiles of potential borrowers. Net income attributable to common shareholder of $13.7 million, compared to $14.7 million in the prior year quarter. Net interest income of $58.1 million, compared to $53.6 million in the prior year quarter. Total non-interest income of $3.0 million in both the current and prior year quarters. Net interest margin of 8.46%, compared to 8.55% in the prior year quarter. Recreation loan originations grew 60% from the prior year quarter to $228.5 million, and the loan portfolio grew 18% to $1.8 billion. title: Biotech M&A Cooking - 3 $10B+ Deals Cap and Active Quarter

Combined with improving IPO activity and FDA efforts to streamline drug development, the sector's recove
body_text: This discussion focuses on the resurgence of biotech M&A activity and why it may signal improving fundamentals across the healthcare sector rather than speculative enthusiasm. Biotech continues to see strong momentum, with multiple multi-billion-dollar acquisitions highlighting how large pharmaceutical companies are preparing for upcoming patent expirations. Combined with improving IPO activity and FDA efforts to streamline drug development, the sector's recovery appears increasingly driven by innovation and strategic investment—not speculation. Key takeaways: Biotech dealmaking remains robust. AbbVie's ~$11B acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics and GSK's ~$11B purchase of Nuvalent continue a wave of multi-billion-dollar transactions in 2025. Patent expirations are driving acquisitions. Large pharmaceutical companies are using M&A to replenish future revenue streams ahead of major patent cliffs later this decade. Strategic fit matters. Both acquisitions complement the buyers' existing therapeutic expertise, giving investors greater confidence that these deals are about long-term growth rather than financial engineering. The biotech capital markets are reopening. Large IPOs and continued M&A suggest investor appetite has improved after several difficult years for the sector. Fundamentals are leading the recovery. Unlike prior periods driven by easy money and speculation, today's market is being supported by clinical data, strategic acquisitions, and improving industry fundamentals. Regulatory tailwinds may help. The FDA's new "Operation Trailblazer" initiative aims to shorten early-stage drug development timelines, potentially strengthening U.S. biotech innovation and accelerating future pipelines.

title: [Precision Ag | Part 1] What Is Precision AG Technology and How Can Farmers Benefit from It?
summary: Precision agriculture technology helps farmers reduce costs, increase efficiency, protect the environment, and enhance machine performance by using a combination of data analysis, technology, and special components.
body_text: Precision agriculture (PA) is a modern farming method that relies on finding and measuring crop variability within fields. It is a unique way that allows farmers to respond to these variables and apply the right amount of water, fertilizer, and pesticides to each plant. Precision agriculture is sometimes referred to as precision farming, satellite agriculture, as-needed farming, or site-specific crop management (SSCM). This technology has changed the way farmers work by helping them lower costs, increase yields, protect the environment, manage farms better, enhance machine performance, and more. How Does Precision Agriculture Work? Precision agriculture works by using a combination of technology and data analysis to optimize farming practices. This includes the collection of various types of data, including soil samples, terrain, weather conditions, and crop health, followed by the identification of patterns that help in making informed decisions about planting, fertilizing, and harvesting. To put these decisions into action, a number of special components are used to help guide tractors and other farm equipment. Some of the key components are: Receiver: The receiver is a critical component of PA technology, as it receives signals from GPS and other satellites. The receiver provides real-time information about the location and movement of machinery, which helps farmers optimize field operations. Display: The display is the interface through which farmers can interact with the technology. It provides real-time information about the location of machinery, crop health, and other vital data. The display allows farmers to adjust settings and make informed decisions based on the data provided. Guidance Solutions (Machine and Implement): Guidance solutions help farmers maintain consistent paths across the field. This ensures that the machinery applies inputs such as fertilizer and pesticides accurately, reducing the amount of wasted input and the risk of overapplication. Implementation guidance systems provide accurate and precise control over the application of inputs, ensuring that crops receive the correct amount of nutrients. What Are the Benefits of Precision Agriculture? Increased efficiency due to automation and repeatability PA technology uses automation and repeatability to ensure that every production process is optimized for maximum efficiency. This includes precise seed placement, consistent spraying, and accurate irrigation. The use of autonomous machinery also reduces labor costs, increases accuracy, and reduces human error. Lowered costs due to precise seed placement and a lack of manual errors Precision technology reduces the costs of inputs such as seeds, fertilizers, and pesticides. By applying these inputs precisely, farmers can reduce the amount needed, which saves money and reduces environmental impact. Additionally, precision technology reduces fuel costs by optimizing machinery movements and reducing the number of passes required. Improvement of every production process translates to higher yields PA technology provides farmers with real-time data on crop health, soil moisture, and weather patterns. This data helps farmers make informed decisions about when to plant, irrigate, fertilize, and harvest. With this knowledge, farmers can improve crop yield and quality, resulting in higher profits. In Conclusion Precision agriculture technology offers numerous benefits to farmers. By using a combination of data analysis, technology, and special components, farmers can optimize every production process, reduce costs, increase efficiency, protect the environment, and enhance machine performance. With real-time data on crop health, soil moisture, and weather patterns, farmers can make informed decisions that result in higher yields and profits. Overall, precision agriculture technology has revolutionized the farming industry and is an essential tool for modern-day farmers. * For more information about John Deere’s precision ag products, you can contact your local John Deere dealers or leave your inquiry through our Contact us form.

title: Autopilot: How our powerful technology drives unmatched sleep improvement
summary: At the core of Eight Sleep lies the belief that technology can help people sleep better. How? We believe that in order to sleep better each individual has to fulfill their own needs.
body_text: At the core of Eight Sleep lies the belief that technology can help people sleep better. How? We believe that in order to sleep better each individual has to fulfill their own needs. So if your bed can understand what you need and address that, then the score will take care of itself. The Pod is more than what you can see When you receive the Pod you unbox a few different components of the product, which you place in your bedroom. This includes the Hub and the Cover. These components are key to your new sleep journey, however, they aren’t sufficient to deliver the full impact on your sleep quality. Behind the Pod, or better said, powering every key function of the Pod is Autopilot: a set of proprietary algorithms developed by Eight Sleep to create an individual blueprint of each sleeper to create the environment you need for your best sleep. How Autopilot helps you get a perfect night’s sleep In a single night, Autopilot takes over 20 actions to help you fall asleep faster, get more deep sleep, and wake up refreshed. Here’s a look into what happens behind the scenes. Step 1: Over a dozen sensors within the Pod detect as you fall asleep and go through sleep stages The Pod features a unique set of imperceptible sensors that detect biometric, presence, and environmental data across the Cover and Hub. These sensors, mostly located within the Pod’s Cover, are sensitive enough to measure signals without direct contact to the skin and are designed seamlessly to feel invisible to the human touch. In addition to how invisible they are, the Pod’s sensors are unique because they function like a wearable without having to be worn. And, unlike wearables, they can track the two people at the same time. Think of it as a BOGO! You get one product, and receive the value for two people. Using the high-quality data gathered from the sensors, Autopilot runs a collection of complex algorithms that compute metrics including the following: Time you fell asleep Time you woke up Heart Rate Variability (HRV) Resting Heart Rate Respiratory Rate Sleep Phases (Deep, REM, Light) Step 2: Autopilot creates an individual blueprint of your sleep needs and solutions The Autopilot algorithms go beyond metrics tracking, to create a profile – or what we call a blueprint – of each individual as a sleeper. Trained on 1.2 million hours of sleep, these algorithms require complex processing to correlate multiple variables into one dynamic picture of who you are as a sleeper and what you need to get the best rest possible. What makes your Autopilot blueprint stand out is that it’s ever changing. It is continuously refined to account for the latest findings on what determines and influences a great night of sleep for you. Your Autopilot blueprint understands your needs, by looking at factors including: Amount of deep sleep you need tonight based on last night’s sleep Amount of REM sleep you need tonight based on last night’s sleep Your current sleep stage Changes in your environmental temperature Your preferred bed temperature at each phase throughout the night Your biological sex Your age Step 3: Autopilot makes real-time adjustments to give you deeper, higher-quality sleep Autopilot was designed with the scientific knowledge that temperature is the #1 environmental factor impacting sleep. That’s why Autopilot primarily relies on temperature adjustments to help you get deeper more restful sleep. With your blueprint in hand and thanks to more than dozens training experiments, Autopilot can determine your optimal sleep temperature at every point of the night and makes automatic adjustments to your Pod by cooling or warming each side without any manual effort from you. This lets you spend more time asleep, and less time guessing what temperature to set at night. This automation and personalization is what ultimately makes the experience of sleeping on a Pod extremely impactful. Did you know? Men and women have different temperature needs due to differences in metabolism and hormones. Autopilot tailors your temperature tonight to compensate for the specific sleep stages you were lacking last night. Autopilot takes your preferences into account when making adjustments. The best part: Autopilot automates all its actions to make your life as easy as possible. Autopilot delivers the ultimate sleep experience with minimal effort required from you. Its automatic features make better sleep simple – just let Autopilot take the wheel. Step 4: Autopilot wakes you up gently and more refreshed Autopilot wakes you up with a gentle vibration and thermal alarm. This wake-up experience is unlike any other, designed to wake you up refreshed without disturbing your partner. Step 5: Autopilot creates a daily report so you can track your sleep progress In the morning, Autopilot wakes you up gently with vibration or temperature and sends your sleep and health data to the app. While Autopilot computes metrics in real-time, once your sleep session has ended the final metrics are summarized into a daily report to help you stay on top of your overall health. The report is centered around your Sleep Fitness Score, which is computed based on sleep quality, routine consistency, and time slept. Clinically validated algorithms, as accurate as medical-grade devices* Validated by thousands of nights of data, Autopilot’s HR and HRV algorithms are 99% and 93% accurate* respectively. *These health-tracking algorithms are constantly being improved and clinically tested by our Research and Development team using gold-standard testing methods like ECGs. Our team has collected over 5,000 nights of data to train, enhance, and test each one of our algorithms and we will continue to refine them as our data set grows over time. Read our studies The world’s best sleep will only keep getting better We’re continuously working to improve Autopilot’s intelligence so that our members can see more sleep improvement. We recently launched Autopilot 3.0 , which automatically adjusts based on your last night’s sleep stages to maximize your sleep performance tonight. Stay on the lookout for more new Autopilot features in the coming months.

body_text: ServisFirst Bancshares, Inc. Announces Results for Second Quarter of 2026 July 20, 2026 4:04pm EDT Download as PDF Related Documents Earnings Webcast Audio BIRMINGHAM, Ala., July 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ServisFirst Bancshares, Inc. (NYSE: SFBS), today announced earnings and operating results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Highlights: Diluted earnings per share of $1.57 for the quarter, up 40% from the second quarter of 2025, and up 30% from adjusted diluted earnings per share in the second quarter of 2025*. Loans grew $533 million, or 15% annualized, during the quarter. Net interest margin of 3.63%, up 10 basis points from the first quarter of 2026 and up 53 basis points from the second quarter of 2025. Book value per share of $36.19, up 14.8% year-over-year. Efficiency ratio under 30%, down from 33% in the second quarter of 2025. About ServisFirst Bancshares, Inc. ServisFirst Bancshares, Inc. (the “Company”) is a bank holding company based in Birmingham, Alabama. Sharing completed projects, customer testimonials, and electrical safety tips keeps your business top of mind. Start with the area that’s costing you the most jobs, then build from there. Get Found First: Local Listings & Google Business Profile for Electricians Customers can’t hire your business if they never see it on Google Maps, in local search results, or in online directories. One of the fastest ways to improve your visibility is by making sure your Google Business Profile and online listings are complete, accurate, and consistent wherever homeowners search. Your Google Business Profile is often the first thing a potential customer sees. Define the cities, neighbourhoods, and local areas you serve. Add recent photos of completed work, service vehicles, and your team. Keep your business hours up to date, especially during holidays or emergencies. Make sure your phone number and website are correct. title: Two Rights Deals in Two Weeks, and the Map Keeps Splitting
summary: The Bundesliga landed on free streaming in the US and a brand new women's baseball league debuted on ESPN, both within a fortnight. Carriage is no longer the bottleneck in sports media. Content throughput is.
body_text: Back to Blog BLOG July 30, 2026 Two Rights Deals in Two Weeks, and the Map Keeps Splitting Two rights announcements landed in the last sixteen days, and taken together they say more about where sports media is heading than either does alone. On July 14, USA Sports and the Bundesliga announced an exclusive multi-year agreement making USA the English language home of German football in the United States. The deal runs through the 2030-31 season and starts next month with more than 300 live matches a year. At least 30 will air on USA Network. Every remaining match streams free on Fandango. Today, the Women's Pro Baseball League debuts. Its inaugural season is carried by ESPN, which distributes the regular season and playoffs in the US, alongside the Scripps Sports Network, which takes a select slate with eleven games simulcast across both. The league is four teams playing fifteen regular season games each, all of them at Robin Roberts Stadium in Springfield, Illinois. What these two have in common One is a hundred and twenty year old league with a global audience. The other played its first professional game this afternoon. Both just secured national US distribution, and neither did it through the mechanism that used to matter, which was convincing a cable operator to carry a channel. The Bundesliga is putting the overwhelming majority of its inventory behind no paywall at all. The WPBL got to ESPN in its first season, something that would have taken a decade of proving itself under the old model. Carriage has stopped being scarce. What is scarce now is a reason for anyone to show up. That reason is almost never the schedule. Nobody discovers a league by browsing a listings grid. They discover it because a clip reached them, and the clip reached them because somebody cut it quickly enough to ride the moment. Where this breaks More than 300 Bundesliga matches a year for a US audience is a serious content obligation, and the American operation servicing it is not the German one. The WPBL is fifteen games per team with a staff that has to build an audience from zero while the season is happening, not afterward. This is the pattern across every new deal signed this year. Rights are fragmenting downward, into more leagues, more windows and more free streaming tiers. Each new window is another surface that needs its own clips, its own cut-downs and its own vertical versions. The teams selling these deals are getting good at it. The teams servicing them are the constraint. At Narrative Sports , we built the layer that makes this survivable. Our platform takes the live feed, identifies the moments worth publishing, and produces finished clips in under 30 seconds across every format a modern rights deal now implies. Whether you have 300 matches or 30, the throughput problem is the same one. Want to see how Narrative Sports can help your team? We help sports teams and broadcasters turn live games into social-ready highlights automatically. body_text: Northrop Grumman Breaks Ground on New Facility to Support Strategic Deterrence and Advanced Aerospace Missions in Utah July 14, 2026 PDF Version As the largest defense contractor in Utah, the company marks a pivotal moment for growth, aerospace innovation and national defense investment ROY, Utah, July 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Northrop Grumman (NYSE: NOC) broke ground on a new building at its expansive Roy Innovation Center (RIC), the central campus tailor-made to develop the U.S. Air Force Sentinel Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (ICBM) program and other critical aerospace and defense missions. Northrop Grumman’s investment to expand the footprint of the Sentinel program will create hundreds of new jobs and supports the accelerated timeline to deliver Sentinel initial capability to the U.S. Air Force by the early 2030s while enabling long-term growth across multiple national security programs. The new addition brings the RIC campus to a total of six state-of-the-art buildings and more than 1.1 million square feet of office space, providing capacity for more than 5,000 employees supporting strategic deterrence and advanced aerospace programs. Construction of the new Legacy Building begins this summer and will be completed by 2028. As the largest defense contractor in Utah, Northrop Grumman’s continued investments in the state are having a significant economic impact while creating hundreds of new jobs across multiple missions and programs. Northrop Grumman directly employs over 11,000 Utahns and, according to a recent study, supports more than 46,000 jobs across the state, generating over $12.4 billion for the economy. Tony Nolls, Director of Operations, Northrop Grumman; Taylor Woodbury, CEO, Woodbury Construction; Sarah Willoughby, Vice President and General Manager, Sentinel Program Director, Northrop Grumman; Spencer J. Cox, Utah Governor; Ben Davies, Corp. Vice President & President, Defense Systems, Northrop Grumman; Amanda Davis, Vice President and Sentinel EMD Program Manager, Northrop Grumman; Joshua Johnson, Vice President of Business Management, Northrop Grumman. (Photo Credit: Northrop Grumman) "As Utah's largest aerospace and defense employer, Northrop Grumman is a cornerstone of our state's economy and a key contributor to our nation's security. We are proud to partner with Northrop Grumman as it advances aerospace innovation, strengthens advanced manufacturing, and creates high-quality jobs across Utah. Together, we are ensuring Utah remains a leader in the technologies and capabilities that support our national defense. For generations, Utah has embraced the responsibility of advancing the strategic deterrence mission, and we are proud to uphold and continue that legacy," said Utah Governor Spencer Cox. “Utah’s world-class talent pool, strategic location to Hill Air Force Base and supportive community make it the ideal home for this expansion of Sentinel and other critical missions we support from this site,” said Ben Davies, corporate vice president and president, Northrop Grumman Defense Systems. “This groundbreaking symbolizes our longstanding commitment to the state and reinforces our investment in national security and local prosperity through an enduring presence that will support multiple missions for decades to come.” Over the past five years, Northrop Grumman has invested $13.5 billion in infrastructure and R&D, including $2 billion dedicated to solid rocket motor capacity and capabilities—that accelerate and scale production for the Sentinel program and strengthen the broader strategic deterrence and space launch industrial base. As Sentinel continues to advance, Northrop Grumman remains focused on delivering warfighter capabilities that balance breakthrough technology, affordability and speed across a portfolio of missions that rely on our Utah facilities and teams. Northrop Grumman is a leading global aerospace and defense technology company. Our pioneering solutions equip our customers with the capabilities they need to connect and protect the world and push the boundaries of human exploration across the universe. Driven by a shared purpose to solve our customers’ toughest problems, our employees define possible every day. title: Resale Certificates: Who Qualifies and How to Obtain One
summary: Resale certificates are documents that a business can supply to a vendor when they are purchasing goods, services, or property that will be resold.
body_text: And this makes dealing with sales tax more complicated. If your business is reselling items to your customers, understanding resale certificates is key. As a sales tax professional, I’ve had the privilege of providing my clients guidance on many different elements of sales tax. In this article, I’ll be covering resale certificates and who can get them. What is a resale certificate? Resale certificates are documents that a business can supply to a vendor when they are purchasing goods, services, or property that will be resold or re-rented to their customers. This allows the business to avoid paying a sales tax (and, at the same time, prevents items from being taxed twice). Resale certificates are used in business-to-business transactions, and they help ensure that those transactions are cost-efficient. Businesses that are reselling goods will need to have a resale certificate to avoid sales tax if they would otherwise have a tax obligation in their location or their customers. Resale certificates are essential because they help reduce the costs of goods and services for a business. A state agency will supply or provide guidance concerning resale certificates and how they can be accessed. Resale certificates are not to be confused with exemption certificates , which allow purchases to be exempt even if they are not resold. There are many eligibility considerations involved with exemption certificates, such as the type of goods being purchased, and whether the items are being purchased by an exempt entity. Please note that some exemption certificates include a blanket form that allows purchasers to identify the exemption reason, which could also include resold items. It’s important to understand and follow the relevant state’s procedures and complete the appropriate documentation. Who can get a resale certificate? Resale certificates are generally used in business-to-business transactions by retailers, wholesalers , and manufacturers . These types of businesses typically qualify for a resale certificate because the items will not be used or consumed but will be resold to an end consumer for profit. Requirements for retrieving or using resale certificates vary by state. For example, the Florida Department of Revenue requires that businesses be registered to collect sales tax before they are issued an annual resale certificate . But for several agencies, such as the Arizona Department of Revenue, resale certificates are optional . Resale certificates are considered valid when the required information is included within a written document. Several state agencies will also allow the use of a Uniform Sales & Use Tax Resale Certificate or a Streamlined Sales Tax Agreement Certificate of Exemption that contains all of the proper exemption documentation needed for a resale. Several state agencies allow the use of your home state registration number, bypassing registration in that state. These are some of the top scenarios where resale certificates may not be needed or applicable: Items that will be used or consumed by the purchaser. Sales tax cannot be avoided for purchases of items that will be used by you and your employees. Purchasing items that do not meet the description of your business operations. It will be difficult to convince a state agency that purchased car parts will be resold to customers of an ice cream shop. (These purchases are not to be confused with items that are part of a casual sale.) Items purchased within a casual sale. These items are typically sold via yard sales and liquidation sales. A business could also sell depreciated equipment or retired furniture when moving to a new location. Why is a resale certificate important? Resale certificates allow a business or its representatives to purchase items that they intend to resell to their customers, without having to pay sales tax. This saves the business money and may allow it to sell goods at a more competitive price. Vendors are obligated to charge sales tax on taxable goods, property, or services when a resale certificate does not exist. In situations where registration is mandatory to retrieve a resale certificate, you must understand the associated legal obligations. Registration signifies that your business will comply with that state’s rules and will charge and collect sales tax, and it gives your business nexus in that state. Your business will need to ensure that your goods, services, or property are not taxable within the state. These duties do have associated administrative costs. The obligation will also leave you open to potential audits, which could be a costly nightmare for any company, significantly more for a small business. How to obtain a resale certificate For many businesses, obtaining a resale certificate is a good idea, but the process varies from state to state and can take a while. In general, these are the steps: Register within the related or your home state for sales tax. Registration may include paying a fee. Registering requires that you provide not only business information, but also the owner’s or an officer’s personal information, such as their home address and social security number. It’s also important to understand your business and its proper categorization, such as the NAICS, first day of taxable sales, and how it impacts related tax types within the state. Access the provided resale certificate. As noted above, certain states provide completed resale certificates that can be accessed once you’re registered. Complete the optional resale exemption form or create a written document that includes the required elements. Certain states have optional forms that can be used for resale exemptions and will allow the use of the Uniform Sales & Use Tax Resale Certificate, Streamlined Sales Tax Agreement Certificate of Exemption, or written document including the required information. Processing time and cost vary by state. Most states allow online registrations for a more efficient process. A completed and approved sales tax permit can be processed immediately or may take as long as four weeks. How to use a resale certificate properly Once you’ve registered, you’re ready to use your resale certificate. Remember, resale certificates can be issued to vendors when the vendor has a sales tax obligation in an origin or destination state. Submitting your resale certificate when your account with a vendor is created is a good business practice that saves a lot of headache and confusion down the road. If you can’t submit it at that time, contact your vendor’s customer service to submit it. It’s important that each business exercise good recordkeeping and documentation on their end to substantiate their exempt sales when needed. Resale certificates' validity periods vary, so it’s also important to maintain records as long as they are valid. Best business practices dictate a recordkeeping period of four to five years, but some businesses hold on to their documentation past this point. Each business must understand state-specific requirements, its state’s statute of limitations for audits, business contract terms, and the regulations of their industry. Renewals of resale certificates vary by state. Some state agencies automatically renew annually and will provide an updated certificate for your use without request, while other agencies may dictate that you complete another pre-filled or written document when the validity period has expired. Vendors may have their own renewal processes — for instance, a vendor may request a resale certificate each year, for their own records. If you are presented with a resale certificate If a business presents a resale certificate to you, the vendor, you should make sure that you verify the certificate before accepting it. A valid resale certificate will have the business name, address, registration number, property description, exemption requirements, declaration, date, and signature. After accepting the certificate, you should maintain a copy of the certificate and put a process in place to track expiration and renewals. If, for any reason, you, the vendor, accept an invalid certificate, the sales tax liability will fall to you and not the customer. States provide different ways to verify resale certificates . Some can be done online, while others require you to call. If you find yourself receiving an increasingly large number of resale certificates from customers, you could explore implementing an exemption certificate management solution , such as the one offered by Numeral. [inline-cta title="Let us worry about sales tax." text="The fastest, easiest way to stay compliant with US sales tax and global VAT. " button="Book a demo" button-link="/demo"] Common mistakes and misconceptions These common misconceptions about resale certificates can get your business in trouble with state agencies or vendors. Misuse of resale certificates could lead to a state audit and additional tax due. Misconception 1: Resale certificates can be used for non-business purchases. ‍ Misconception 2: Resale certificates can be used for purchases that will not be resold. ‍ Misconception 3: It is not important to completely fill out the pre-filled forms or include all required documentation in a written document. Special cases and exceptions There are special cases and exceptions to every rule. Please consult your specific industry and state agency to learn about any anomalies. Frequently asked questions Can an individual get a resale certificate? Yes! Individuals can receive a resale certificate if the qualifications are met. Requirements vary by state. Some states that will accept an individual’s resale certificates are California, Georgia, and Texas. Can online businesses also use resale certificates? Online businesses can use resale certificates, with the understanding that the items are to be resold in the regular course of business. Do resale certificates apply to services? In some cases, taxable services can be purchased without tax and resold. Examples are installation services, construction services, and professional services. Review the relevant state’s policies to ensure that services can be resold and to understand the documentation needed to validate the sale. How do you confirm whether a vendor accepts resale certificates? The most efficient path for confirmation is to submit a completed resale certificate when an account is created for your business. If there is not an opportunity to provide a resale certificate in the initial phase, a business can follow up with the vendor’s customer support team to adjust the invoice. Do resale certificates expire? Each state has rules pertaining to the validity of exemption certificates. Some states will issue an annual resale exemption certificate for use, while other state agencies will allow the use of the certificate indefinitely. Best business practices typically include a review cycle ranging from annually to every three years. Which states do not accept out-of-state resale certificates? Here is a complete list . The bottom line Resale certificates allow qualified businesses and individuals to purchase goods, services, or property for resale, without paying sales tax. The documents avoid double taxation and save businesses money. Requirements and obligations involved with resale certificates vary by state, and it’s important to consult with a tax professional or an applicable state agency if additional information or guidance is required.

title: Managing Rising Carbide Costs: Maximize Tool Value — MSC Industrial Supply Co.
summary: Carbide costs are climbing fast. Learn how to calculate true cost per edge, extend tool life, and work smarter with suppliers to protect your bottom line.
body_text: Whether it’s a solid carbide end mill, a pack of indexable inserts or a few replacement tips for that new modular drill, higher costs have come to the tool crib. The biggest driver behind this phenomenon is one that some manufacturing professionals may not consider: the rising cost of tungsten carbide and the other raw materials used in cutting tool production, all of which are squeezing margins for machine shops and suppliers alike. As a result of this inflationary pressure, purchasing managers and shop supervisors are looking for ways to cut costs, which is an effort that starts by treating carbide tooling as a managed asset rather than a consumable. “Lower-cost inserts may sound like a good choice up-front, but inconsistent tool life or unexpected breakage can quickly drive up the real cost in production.” Bill Koscelnik, Senior Manager of National Distribution, Kennametal But cutting costs doesn’t have to mean cutting performance. From calculating the true cost per edge to determining the right speeds, feeds and toolpaths, it’s possible to achieve maximum productivity from every carbide dollar. For advice, we turned to Bill Koscelnik, Kennametal’s senior manager of national distribution, and Dan Tucker, SE product specialist-SAA with Sandvik Coromant US. They both had plenty to say about cutting tool costs while offering some tips on why shops should recondition or at least recycle that tired cutter, and why supplier partnerships outperform spot buys. Why Carbide Costs Are Rising: Understanding the Supply Chain Pressure Before we talk about fixing the problem, let’s do what any lean-minded shop would do and run a quick root cause analysis. Think of it as a round of the “5 whys,” starting with the most basic question of all: Why are carbide costs climbing in the first place? Tucker points to severe Chinese export controls, coupled with environmental crackdowns that cut mining output by more than 6 percent, as a driving factor. “In addition, we’ve seen explosive growth in the military and defense sector; panic buying and stockpiling; and surging demand from high-tech industry, electric vehicles, oil and gas drilling and quantum computing,” he says. The result? Since early 2025, tungsten powder prices have more than doubled. With that, ammonium paratungstate (APT), the core chemical intermediate used in cemented carbide production, leaped from $335 to $1,100 per MTU. Another key ingredient—cobalt—spiked more than 200 percent. “Add it all up, and the cemented carbide rods used to make most solid round tools are rising 80 percent year over year,” Tucker says. Video: Why Tungsten Carbide is SO EXPENSIVE Lately Calculating Your True Cost Per Edge: The Metric That Matters Most Koscelnik begins with a brief explanation of this critical yet often misunderstood (or at least misapplied) metric. “At a basic level, cost per edge is pretty straightforward: the cost of the insert divided by the number of usable cutting edges,” he says. To measure the true cost per edge, he says, you need to consider other factors such as tool life and tool quality. “For example, lower-cost inserts may sound like a good choice up-front, but inconsistent tool life or unexpected breakage can quickly drive up the real cost in production,” Koscelnik says. “So my advice to customers is to look at durability, consistency and application fit to get a much better picture of overall value to make informed tooling decisions.” Tucker agrees, noting that inserts in certain indexable cutters may have a higher cost per edge but deliver far greater output. Consider a CoroMill MS20 square-shoulder face mill. As its name suggests, this solution can perform face milling, shoulder milling, ramping, helical interpolation and pocket milling. But with only two corners and a price tag of roughly $30 per insert, the cost per edge is $15. Now compare that to the eight-sided inserts in a CoroMill MF80, which sell for about the same price. The cost per edge here drops to $3.75, yet the cutter is primarily for higher-volume work, where cost per edge is the top consideration. “If you’re only facing, then the MF80 will be the most economical choice without giving up productivity. Otherwise, shops should consider the greater flexibility and performance gains they’ll get with cutters like the MS20, with geometries designed for demanding applications,” Tucker says. Extending Carbide Tool Life With the Right Speeds and Feeds Most cutting tool providers recommend visiting their websites for the correct cutting parameters, and Kennametal is no different. As Koscelnik points out, spindle speeds too high for the application generate excessive heat and rapid edge wear. Run too low and the tool rubs instead of cutting, which again leads to shortened tool life and breakage. Feed rate has a similar effect. “Each insert geometry requires that you push the tool hard enough for proper chip formation—go too slow and the insert rubs rather than cuts; too fast and it can chip or break,” he says. “As for depth of cut (DOC), it’s much like feed rate—a factor of the insert geometry, as well as setup rigidity, workpiece material and so on—which is why selecting the correct insert for the desired DOC is essential for any machining application.” Like Kennametal, the Sandvik Coromant website is replete with feed and speed calculators and cutting tool recommendations. And while Tucker fully supports tool life and process improvement, he warns against pushing tools too hard. Doing so can lead to accelerated wear and tear on the machine, elevated component costs and the risk of catastrophic part damage, not to mention the need for expensive premium tooling and extensive trial and error while operators dial in the process. His recommendation? “Aim for 80 percent efficiency,” Tucker says. “In other words, run tools at 80 percent of the max recommendation. Even backing off 10 to 15 percent might yield a 50 percent increase in tool life. With that, it’s important to refresh or change tools at a predictable part count versus running to failure. Prioritize predictability.” Video: How to Maximize Carbide Efficiency Why OEM Reconditioning Beats Third-Party Regrinding Tucker says shops should also prioritize tool reconditioning, but do it the right way. “The common mistake small- to mid-sized shops make is using a local grinding house for tool resharpening, which must then reverse engineer the geometry and coatings. Though it might be cheaper, it comes at a cost of ‘not like new’ performance,” Tucker says. “By comparison, the grinders and coating chambers Sandvik Coromant uses for reconditioning are the same equipment that made the tools in the first place, so we guarantee like-new performance.” Carbide Recycling Programs: How to Turn Scrap Tooling Into Credit Koscelnik is also a fan of tool reconditioning, noting that high-performance drills and end mills can easily achieve tool life close to that of new, but at a much lower cost. For a commodity tool, however, it often makes more sense to replace it with a new one and send the scrap carbide back to Kennametal for recycling . “It’s a great way to turn used tools into cash while also contributing to greener manufacturing,” he says. Tucker seconds this. “With the price of recycled carbide at around $32 per pound, it only makes sense,” he says. “After all, 50 pounds of carbide is nearly $1,600, which is money that goes right to your company’s bottom line.” Vendor Partnership vs. Spot Buying: Why Your Supplier Relationship Affects Cost The two agree on several additional points, one of them being the need for strong partnerships with their customers. “With a supplier relationship, you often get more consistent and lower costs, versus spot buying where you can easily pay a premium price,” Koscelnik says. According to Tucker, “spot buys” may give shops the flexibility to purchase from whomever they desire, but doing so most likely comes at higher prices and with the risk of stock being unavailable. “If we know company XYZ is going to use 2,000 inserts in a year, a formal long-term agreement means we can manufacture the needed inventory ahead of time, dedicate it to that customer and ensure they get the best possible pricing,” Tucker says. “On the flip side, no agreement means we’ll adjust our inventory levels based upon current market demand, so those inserts might not be there when the customer places their order.” The Hidden Costs of Stockpiling Carbide (And a Better Approach) Of course, shops unwilling to commit can always do what Tucker suggested earlier was one of the root causes of rising carbide costs: stockpile cutting tools. This practice might avoid the potential stock-out just mentioned, but it comes with other costs: Locks up much-needed working capital. Leads to material degradation and damage, such as physical chipping of the carbide. Ties the shop into old technology when new advancements are released. Typically increases inventory holding costs by 20 percent to 30 percent. The answer? “Work with your suppliers to develop buying agreements that benefit both parties, and ensure that cutting tools will be there when needed,” Tucker says. “This yields the best pricing and delivery security.” Koscelnik offers an alternative path. “I’d point them to our ToolBOSS vending system to help build and manage inventory while maximizing productivity. It tracks tooling usage in real time and can also be set to calculate demand, place orders automatically and more.”
